sections.title: The cardiovascular system & two circulations
sections.highlight: The heart is two pumps: the RIGHT side sends blood to the lungs (pulmonary circulation); the LEFT side sends blood to all other tissues (systemic circulation).

sections.title: Functions, size & location of the heart
sections.highlight: Base = top, directed to the right and superiorly (behind the sternum to the 2nd intercostal space). Apex = bottom, directed to the left and inferiorly (5th intercostal space).

sections.title: Pericardium & its disorders
sections.highlight: Fibrous pericardium (outer, tough) → serous pericardium: PARIETAL lines the fibrous layer, VISCERAL (epicardium) sits on the heart. Fluid in the cavity between them reduces friction.

sections.title: Blood flow through the heart
sections.highlight: Venae cavae → RA → tricuspid → RV → pulmonary semilunar valve → pulmonary trunk → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → LA → bicuspid → LV → aortic semilunar valve → aorta → body.

sections.title: Cardiac muscle & the contraction sequence
sections.highlight: Intercalated disks with gap junctions join cardiac cells physically AND electrically. Atria contract first; ventricles are then stimulated from the apex toward the base.

sections.title: Cardiac muscle action potentials
sections.highlight: Depolarization: Na⁺ + Ca²⁺ channels open. Plateau: Na⁺ closes, Ca²⁺ stays open (some K⁺ opens). Repolarization: K⁺ open, Ca²⁺ closes. Long AP (200–500 ms vs 2 ms) + refractory period = no tetany.

sections.title: Conduction system of the heart
sections.highlight: SA node (pacemaker, in RA) → AV node (slow, so the atria finish contracting) → AV bundle → right & left bundle branches (down the septum) → Purkinje fibers (fast delivery to the ventricles).

sections.title: Electrocardiogram (ECG)
sections.highlight: P wave = atrial depolarization. QRS complex = ventricular depolarization (also leads to atrial relaxation). T wave = ventricular repolarization.

sections.title: The cardiac cycle
sections.highlight: Blood moves from high to low pressure. Relaxed heart: AV valves open, SL valves closed. Ventricular systole: AV valves close → SL valves open. Ventricular diastole: SL valves close → AV valves open.

sections.title: Heart sounds
sections.highlight: Lubb (first sound) = AV valves close. Dupp (second sound) = semilunar valves close. Murmurs = incompetent or stenosed valves.

sections.title: Cardiac output & intrinsic regulation
sections.highlight: CO = SV × HR (70 mL/beat × 72 beats/min ≈ 5 L/min). Starling's law: ↑ venous return → ↑ stretch (preload) → stronger contraction → ↑ SV and CO. Afterload = pressure the ventricles pump against.

sections.title: Extrinsic regulation: baroreceptor & chemoreceptor reflexes
sections.highlight: ↓ BP → baroreceptors (aorta, internal carotids) fire less → medulla ↑ sympathetic, ↓ parasympathetic (+ adrenal epi/NE) → ↑ HR, SV, CO → BP rises. Medulla chemoreceptors: ↓ pH/↑ CO₂ → ↑ HR and SV.

sections.title: Heart disease
sections.highlight: Coronary artery disease = narrowed coronary arteries → less blood to the heart. MI = closure of a coronary artery → muscle dies and scars (infarct).

sections.title: Heart extras: MI panel, procedures & aging
sections.highlight: Angioplasty opens vessels, stents keep them open, bypass reroutes blood. With age, CO falls by one-third by age 70.

sections.title: Blood components & plasma proteins
sections.highlight: Plasma 55% (91% water, 7% protein, 2% other) + formed elements 45%. Plasma proteins: albumin 58% (water balance), globulins 38% (immunity, transport), fibrinogen 4% (clotting). Serum = plasma without clotting factors.

sections.title: Hematopoiesis
sections.highlight: One hemocytoblast → MYELOID line (RBC, platelets via megakaryocyte, neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil, monocyte) or LYMPHOID line (lymphocytes). After birth: mainly red bone marrow.

sections.title: Red blood cells, hemoglobin & CO₂ transport
sections.highlight: Biconcave, no nucleus, lives 110–120 days, one-third hemoglobin. Each globin is attached to a heme with one iron that binds O₂ (oxyhemoglobin). CO binds Hb more readily than O₂. CO₂: 70% bicarbonate, 23% on globin, 7% dissolved.

sections.title: RBC production & breakdown
sections.highlight: ↓ blood O₂ → kidneys ↑ erythropoietin → red marrow ↑ RBCs → O₂ rises (negative feedback). Breakdown: macrophages in spleen/liver; globin → amino acids; iron recycled; heme → bilirubin → liver → bile → feces (some urine).

sections.title: White blood cells
sections.highlight: Granulocytes: NEUTROPHIL (most common, 2–4 lobes, phagocyte, pus), EOSINOPHIL (bright red granules, 2 lobes, worms, ↓ inflammation), BASOPHIL (least common, blue/purple, histamine + heparin). Agranulocytes: LYMPHOCYTE (T & B cells, antibodies), MONOCYTE (largest → macrophages).

sections.title: Platelets, vascular spasm & the platelet plug
sections.highlight: Three ways to limit blood loss: vascular spasm → platelet plug → coagulation. Plug: platelets ADHERE to exposed collagen → ACTIVATE (change shape, release chemicals, express fibrinogen receptors) → AGGREGATE via fibrinogen bridges.

sections.title: Coagulation & clot control
sections.highlight: Injury → active clotting factors (+ Ca²⁺ and platelet chemicals) → PROTHROMBINASE → prothrombin → THROMBIN → fibrinogen → FIBRIN (clot). Clotting factors: made in the liver, need vitamin K. Fibrinolysis: plasminogen → plasmin.

sections.title: ABO blood groups & transfusion
sections.highlight: Type A: A antigen + anti-B. Type B: B antigen + anti-A. Type AB: both antigens, no antibodies (universal recipient). Type O: no antigens, both antibodies (universal donor).

sections.title: Rh group & hemolytic disease of the newborn
sections.highlight: Rh⁻ mother + Rh⁺ fetus: the first exposure sensitizes her (antibodies form). In a later pregnancy her anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta → agglutination & hemolysis of fetal RBCs (HDN). Prevent with RhoGAM.

sections.title: Blood extras: ABO distribution & typing photo
sections.highlight: Type O is the most common type in both US groups shown on the slide (47% and 46%).

sections.title: Circuits, vessel types & the direction of flow
sections.highlight: Arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart, veins carry it TOWARD the heart, and capillaries are where exchange happens. Heart → elastic arteries → muscular arteries → arterioles → capillaries → venules → small → medium → large veins → heart.

sections.title: Vessel walls & arteries
sections.highlight: Tunica intima = endothelium (simple squamous). Tunica media = smooth muscle + elastin + collagen. Tunica adventitia (externa) = dense connective tissue. Elastic arteries (aorta, pulmonary trunk) → muscular (distributing) arteries → arterioles.

sections.title: Capillaries & veins
sections.highlight: Capillary wall = 1 layer of simple squamous epithelium (for diffusion). Precapillary sphincters control flow in. Large veins have valves to prevent backflow due to gravity.

sections.title: The aorta & aortic arch branches
sections.highlight: Ascending aorta (coronary arteries at its base) → aortic arch: 1) brachiocephalic (→ R common carotid + R subclavian), 2) L common carotid, 3) L subclavian → descending aorta: thoracic (to diaphragm) + abdominal (to the common iliacs).

sections.title: Arteries of the head, neck & upper limb
sections.highlight: Circle of Willis = internal carotids + basilar artery (two vertebrals fuse). Brachial artery = where BP is measured. Radial artery (thumb side) = where the pulse is taken.

sections.title: Branches of the abdominal aorta
sections.highlight: Unpaired visceral: celiac trunk (stomach, pancreas, spleen, liver, upper duodenum), SMA (small intestine + upper colon), IMA (colon). Paired visceral: renal, suprarenal, gonadal. Parietal: inferior phrenic, lumbar.

sections.title: Major veins & the venae cavae
sections.highlight: SVC drains the head, neck, thorax and right upper limbs; IVC drains the abdomen, pelvis and lower limbs. Both empty into the RIGHT ATRIUM.

sections.title: Veins of the head, neck & upper limb
sections.highlight: Jugular veins → subclavian → brachiocephalic → SVC. Median cubital vein (connects to the cephalic vein near the elbow) is used for drawing blood.

sections.title: Hepatic portal system
sections.highlight: Portal system = starts in capillaries of the viscera and ends in capillaries of the liver (splenic + superior mesenteric veins → hepatic portal vein). Then hepatic veins → IVC → right atrium.

sections.title: Blood pressure, resistance & pulse pressure
sections.highlight: Average BP 120/80. Pressure falls to ~0 by the right atrium. Smaller diameter → higher resistance. Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic (120 − 80 = 40 mmHg), affected by SV and compliance.

sections.title: Capillary exchange
sections.highlight: Arterial end: blood pressure > osmotic pressure → fluid OUT. Venous end: osmotic pressure > blood pressure → fluid IN. Not all fluid returns; the excess (Fig 13.20: ~1/10) goes to the lymphatics.

sections.title: Local, nervous & hormonal control of blood flow
sections.highlight: Local: precapillary sphincters respond to metabolic needs (↓ O₂ → relax → ↑ flow). Nervous: vasomotor center → sympathetic → vasomotor tone. Hormonal: epi/NE constrict most vessels but DILATE vessels in skeletal and cardiac muscle.

sections.title: Mean arterial pressure
sections.highlight: MAP = CO × PR, with CO = HR × SV. MAP changes when HR, SV, or PR change. MAP ≈ 70 mmHg at birth, ≈ 95 mmHg from adolescence to middle age, up to 110 mmHg in healthy older people.

sections.title: Baroreceptor & chemoreceptor reflexes (BP)
sections.highlight: Baroreceptors (carotid sinuses, aortic arch) sense stretch and adjust PR, HR, and SV. Chemoreceptors (carotid & aortic bodies) sense O₂, CO₂, and pH and signal the medulla oblongata.

sections.title: Adrenal medullary mechanism
sections.highlight: Stimuli (physical activity, stress) → ↑ sympathetic → adrenal medulla secretes epinephrine & norepinephrine → ↑ HR, SV, vasoconstriction; vasodilation in skeletal and cardiac muscle.

sections.title: Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone mechanism
sections.highlight: ↓ blood flow → kidneys release RENIN → angiotensinogen (liver) → ANGIOTENSIN I → ACE (lung capillaries) → ANGIOTENSIN II → vasoconstriction + ALDOSTERONE (adrenal cortex) → kidneys conserve Na⁺ and water → BP maintained.

sections.title: ADH & atrial natriuretic mechanisms
sections.highlight: ADH (hypothalamus; ↑ solutes or ↓ BP) → kidneys absorb more water → ↓ urine → blood volume & BP maintained. ANH (right atrium; ↑ atrial BP) → kidneys lose Na⁺ & water → ↑ urine → ↓ blood volume & BP.

sections.title: Summary: short-term vs long-term BP regulation
sections.highlight: SHORT-TERM (react quickly to sudden changes): baroreceptor reflexes (most important), chemoreceptor and adrenal medulla reflexes (more for large changes). LONG-TERM (gradual, sensitive to small changes): RAAS, ADH, ANH.

sections.title: Effects of aging on blood vessels
sections.highlight: Arteriosclerosis = arteries become less elastic. Atherosclerosis = a type of arteriosclerosis from plaque deposits in artery walls.

sections.title: Extra arteries: thoracic, pelvic & lower limb
sections.highlight: External iliac → femoral → popliteal → anterior tibial (→ dorsalis pedis) and posterior tibial (→ fibular).

sections.title: Extra veins: thorax, abdomen, pelvis & lower limb
sections.highlight: Posterior intercostals → azygos (right) or hemiazygos/accessory hemiazygos (left) → SVC. Great saphenous = dorsal and medial foot; small saphenous = lateral foot → popliteal.

facts.text: Starling's law of the heart is the relationship between preload and stroke volume.

facts.cloze: If venous return increases, the muscle fibers stretch more and contract with {{c1::greater force}}, increasing SV and CO.
facts.text: If venous return increases, the muscle fibers stretch more and contract with greater force, increasing SV and CO.

facts.cloze: Exercise increases venous return, preload, stroke volume, and {{c1::cardiac output}}.
facts.text: Exercise increases venous return, preload, stroke volume, and cardiac output.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Afterload}} is the pressure against which the ventricles must pump blood.
facts.text: Afterload is the pressure against which the ventricles must pump blood.

facts.cloze: High blood pressure means a {{c1::greater force}} of ventricular contraction is needed to open the SL valves.
facts.text: High blood pressure means a greater force of ventricular contraction is needed to open the SL valves.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Extrinsic regulation}} refers to mechanisms external to the heart, either nervous or chemical.
facts.text: Extrinsic regulation refers to mechanisms external to the heart, either nervous or chemical.

facts.cloze: Both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerve fibers innervate the {{c1::SA node}}.
facts.text: Both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerve fibers innervate the SA node.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Sympathetic}} nerves increase heart rate and stroke volume; {{c2::parasympathetic}} nerves decrease them.
facts.text: Sympathetic nerves increase heart rate and stroke volume; parasympathetic nerves decrease them.

facts.cloze: For heart regulation, baroreceptors monitor blood pressure in the {{c1::aorta}} and {{c2::internal carotid arteries}}.
facts.text: For heart regulation, baroreceptors monitor blood pressure in the aorta and internal carotid arteries.

facts.cloze: Baroreceptor action potentials go to the {{c1::cardioregulatory center}} in the {{c2::medulla oblongata}}.
facts.text: Baroreceptor action potentials go to the cardioregulatory center in the medulla oblongata.

facts.cloze: When BP decreases, baroreceptor stimulation {{c1::decreases}}, triggering increased {{c2::sympathetic}} and decreased {{c3::parasympathetic}} stimulation of the heart.
facts.text: When BP decreases, baroreceptor stimulation decreases, triggering increased sympathetic and decreased parasympathetic stimulation of the heart.

facts.cloze: Sympathetic nerves also cause release of {{c1::epinephrine and norepinephrine}} from the {{c2::adrenal medulla}}.
facts.text: Sympathetic nerves also cause release of epinephrine and norepinephrine from the adrenal medulla.

facts.cloze: In the baroreceptor reflex for low BP, heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output {{c1::increase}}, raising BP; the opposite happens when BP rises.
facts.text: In the baroreceptor reflex for low BP, heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output increase, raising BP; the opposite happens when BP rises.

facts.cloze: Fig 12.23: parasympathetic fibers reach the heart in the {{c1::vagus nerves}}; sympathetic fibers in the {{c2::cardiac nerves}}.
facts.text: Fig 12.23: parasympathetic fibers reach the heart in the vagus nerves; sympathetic fibers in the cardiac nerves.

facts.cloze: Chemoreceptors in the {{c1::medulla oblongata}} respond to changes in {{c2::pH}} and {{c3::CO₂}}.
facts.text: Chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata respond to changes in pH and CO₂.

facts.cloze: Fig 12.22: when blood pH {{c1::decreases}} (often from increased CO₂), control centers increase stimulation of the heart and adrenal medulla, so HR and SV increase.
facts.text: Fig 12.22: when blood pH decreases (often from increased CO₂), control centers increase stimulation of the heart and adrenal medulla, so HR and SV increase.

facts.cloze: Elevated body temperature {{c1::increases}} heart rate; lower temperature {{c2::decreases}} it.
facts.text: Elevated body temperature increases heart rate; lower temperature decreases it.

facts.cloze: Excitement, anxiety and anger can {{c1::increase}} cardiac output; depression can {{c2::decrease}} it.
facts.text: Excitement, anxiety and anger can increase cardiac output; depression can decrease it.

facts.cloze: {{c1::K⁺}}, {{c2::Ca²⁺}}, and {{c3::Na⁺}} affect cardiac function.
facts.text: K⁺, Ca²⁺, and Na⁺ affect cardiac function.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Coronary artery disease}} decreases blood supply to the heart because the coronary arteries are narrowed.
facts.text: Coronary artery disease decreases blood supply to the heart because the coronary arteries are narrowed.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Myocardial infarction}} (heart attack) is due to closure of one or more {{c2::coronary arteries}}.
facts.text: Myocardial infarction (heart attack) is due to closure of one or more coronary arteries.

facts.cloze: In myocardial infarction, cardiac muscle lacking adequate blood supply dies and scars ({{c1::infarct}}).
facts.text: In myocardial infarction, cardiac muscle lacking adequate blood supply dies and scars (infarct).

facts.cloze: {{c1::Angioplasty}} is a procedure that opens blocked blood vessels.
facts.text: Angioplasty is a procedure that opens blocked blood vessels.

facts.cloze: A {{c1::stent}} is a structure inserted to keep vessels open.
facts.text: A stent is a structure inserted to keep vessels open.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Bypass}} reroutes blood away from blocked arteries.
facts.text: Bypass reroutes blood away from blocked arteries.

facts.cloze: Cardiac output decreases by {{c1::one-third}} by age {{c2::70}}.
facts.text: Cardiac output decreases by one-third by age 70.

facts.cloze: With aging the {{c1::left ventricle}} hypertrophies because of increased {{c2::afterload}}.
facts.text: With aging the left ventricle hypertrophies because of increased afterload.

facts.cloze: With aging, valves may become {{c1::stenosed or incompetent}} and cardiac {{c2::arrhythmias}} increase.
facts.text: With aging, valves may become stenosed or incompetent and cardiac arrhythmias increase.

facts.cloze: Exercise has beneficial effects on the heart {{c1::at any age}}.
facts.text: Exercise has beneficial effects on the heart at any age.

facts.cloze: Fig 12.25: a symptom of MI is chest pain that radiates {{c1::down the left arm}}.
facts.text: Fig 12.25: a symptom of MI is chest pain that radiates down the left arm.

facts.cloze: Blood functions include transport, regulation of {{c1::pH and osmosis}}, maintenance of {{c2::body temperature}}, protection against foreign substances, and {{c3::clot formation}}.
facts.text: Blood functions include transport, regulation of pH and osmosis, maintenance of body temperature, protection against foreign substances, and clot formation.

facts.cloze: Plasma is {{c1::55%}} of total blood volume.
facts.text: Plasma is 55% of total blood volume.

facts.cloze: Plasma is a {{c1::pale, yellow}} liquid that surrounds cells.
facts.text: Plasma is a pale, yellow liquid that surrounds cells.

facts.cloze: Plasma is {{c1::91%}} water, {{c2::7%}} proteins, and {{c3::2%}} other.
facts.text: Plasma is 91% water, 7% proteins, and 2% other.

facts.cloze: Formed elements are {{c1::45%}} of total blood.
facts.text: Formed elements are 45% of total blood.

facts.cloze: Formed elements are cells and cell fragments: {{c1::erythrocytes}}, {{c2::leukocytes}}, and {{c3::thrombocytes}}.
facts.text: Formed elements are cells and cell fragments: erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes.

facts.cloze: Red blood cells make up almost {{c1::95%}} of all formed elements.
facts.text: Red blood cells make up almost 95% of all formed elements.

facts.cloze: Fig 11.1: blood makes up about {{c1::8%}} of total body weight.
facts.text: Fig 11.1: blood makes up about 8% of total body weight.

facts.cloze: Fig 11.1: in a centrifuged tube the thin layer between plasma and formed elements is the {{c1::buffy coat}}.
facts.text: Fig 11.1: in a centrifuged tube the thin layer between plasma and formed elements is the buffy coat.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Albumin}} is 58% of plasma proteins and helps maintain {{c2::water balance}}.
facts.text: Albumin is 58% of plasma proteins and helps maintain water balance.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Globulins}} are 38% of plasma proteins; they help the immune system and act as {{c2::transport molecules}}.
facts.text: Globulins are 38% of plasma proteins; they help the immune system and act as transport molecules.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Fibrinogen}} is 4% of plasma proteins and aids in {{c2::clot formation}}.
facts.text: Fibrinogen is 4% of plasma proteins and aids in clot formation.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Serum}} is plasma without the clotting factors.
facts.text: Serum is plasma without the clotting factors.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Hematopoiesis}} is the process that produces formed elements.
facts.text: Hematopoiesis is the process that produces formed elements.

facts.cloze: In the fetus, hematopoiesis occurs in the {{c1::liver, thymus, spleen, lymph nodes, and red bone marrow}}.
facts.text: In the fetus, hematopoiesis occurs in the liver, thymus, spleen, lymph nodes, and red bone marrow.

facts.cloze: After birth, hematopoiesis is confined primarily to {{c1::red bone marrow}}, but some WBCs are produced in {{c2::lymphatic tissues}}.
facts.text: After birth, hematopoiesis is confined primarily to red bone marrow, but some WBCs are produced in lymphatic tissues.

facts.cloze: All formed elements derive from {{c1::hematopoietic stem cells}}, also called {{c2::hemocytoblasts}}.
facts.text: All formed elements derive from hematopoietic stem cells, also called hemocytoblasts.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Myeloid}} stem cells give rise to most formed elements.
facts.text: Myeloid stem cells give rise to most formed elements.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Lymphoid}} stem cells give rise to {{c2::lymphocytes}}.
facts.text: Lymphoid stem cells give rise to lymphocytes.

facts.cloze: Fig 11.2: platelets come from the {{c1::megakaryocyte}}, which arises from the myeloid stem cell.
facts.text: Fig 11.2: platelets come from the megakaryocyte, which arises from the myeloid stem cell.

facts.cloze: Fig 11.2: the {{c1::monocyte}} arises from the myeloid stem cell line.
facts.text: Fig 11.2: the monocyte arises from the myeloid stem cell line.

facts.cloze: RBCs are {{c1::biconcave disks}} with edges thicker than the center.
facts.text: RBCs are biconcave disks with edges thicker than the center.

facts.cloze: RBCs can {{c1::change shape}} as they move through capillaries.
facts.text: RBCs can change shape as they move through capillaries.

facts.cloze: RBCs lose their {{c1::nuclei}} and most organelles during development and are unable to {{c2::divide}}.
facts.text: RBCs lose their nuclei and most organelles during development and are unable to divide.

facts.cloze: RBCs live about {{c1::110–120 days}}.
facts.text: RBCs live about 110–120 days.

facts.cloze: {{c1::One-third}} of RBC volume is hemoglobin, which contains iron and gives RBCs their red color.
facts.text: One-third of RBC volume is hemoglobin, which contains iron and gives RBCs their red color.

facts.cloze: RBCs transport {{c1::O₂}} from the lungs to body tissues and help transport {{c2::CO₂}} back to the lungs.
facts.text: RBCs transport O₂ from the lungs to body tissues and help transport CO₂ back to the lungs.

facts.cloze: Fig 11.3: an RBC is about {{c1::7.5 µm}} across and {{c2::2.0 µm}} thick.
facts.text: Fig 11.3: an RBC is about 7.5 µm across and 2.0 µm thick.

facts.cloze: Each {{c1::globin}} protein is attached to a {{c2::heme}} molecule.
facts.text: Each globin protein is attached to a heme molecule.

facts.cloze: Each heme contains {{c1::one iron atom}}.
facts.text: Each heme contains one iron atom.

facts.cloze: O₂ bound to iron is called {{c1::oxyhemoglobin}}.
facts.text: O₂ bound to iron is called oxyhemoglobin.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Carbon monoxide}} binds hemoglobin more readily than O₂.
facts.text: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin more readily than O₂.

facts.cloze: Fig 11.4: hemoglobin has two {{c1::alpha (α)}} and two {{c2::beta (β)}} globin chains.
facts.text: Fig 11.4: hemoglobin has two alpha (α) and two beta (β) globin chains.

facts.cloze: About {{c1::70%}} of CO₂ is transported as {{c2::bicarbonate ions}}.
facts.text: About 70% of CO₂ is transported as bicarbonate ions.

facts.cloze: Bicarbonate forms in RBCs using the enzyme {{c1::carbonic anhydrase}}: CO₂ + H₂O ↔ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻.
facts.text: Bicarbonate forms in RBCs using the enzyme carbonic anhydrase: CO₂ + H₂O ↔ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻.

facts.cloze: About {{c1::23%}} of CO₂ is transported bound to the {{c2::globin}} protein of hemoglobin.
facts.text: About 23% of CO₂ is transported bound to the globin protein of hemoglobin.

facts.cloze: About {{c1::7%}} of CO₂ is transported dissolved in the plasma.
facts.text: About 7% of CO₂ is transported dissolved in the plasma.

facts.cloze: Decreased blood O₂ causes the {{c1::kidneys}} to increase production of {{c2::erythropoietin}}.
facts.text: Decreased blood O₂ causes the kidneys to increase production of erythropoietin.

facts.cloze: Erythropoietin stimulates the {{c1::red bone marrow}} to produce more erythrocytes.
facts.text: Erythropoietin stimulates the red bone marrow to produce more erythrocytes.

facts.cloze: Hematopoietic stem cells form {{c1::proerythroblasts}} in RBC production.
facts.text: Hematopoietic stem cells form proerythroblasts in RBC production.

facts.cloze: RBC production depends on sufficient {{c1::iron}} and several {{c2::B vitamins}}.
facts.text: RBC production depends on sufficient iron and several B vitamins.

facts.cloze: RBC production is controlled by a {{c1::negative-feedback}} mechanism.
facts.text: RBC production is controlled by a negative-feedback mechanism.

facts.cloze: Fig 11.5: the stage just before a mature RBC is the {{c1::reticulocyte}}; the nucleus is extruded after the {{c2::late erythroblast}} stage.
facts.text: Fig 11.5: the stage just before a mature RBC is the reticulocyte; the nucleus is extruded after the late erythroblast stage.

facts.cloze: Old RBCs are removed from blood by {{c1::macrophages}} in the {{c2::spleen and liver}}.
facts.text: Old RBCs are removed from blood by macrophages in the spleen and liver.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Globin}} is broken down into {{c2::amino acids}}.
facts.text: Globin is broken down into amino acids.

facts.cloze: Hemoglobin's {{c1::iron}} is recycled.
facts.text: Hemoglobin's iron is recycled.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Heme}} is converted to {{c2::bilirubin}}.
facts.text: Heme is converted to bilirubin.

facts.cloze: Bilirubin is taken up by the {{c1::liver}} and released into the small intestine as part of {{c2::bile}}.
facts.text: Bilirubin is taken up by the liver and released into the small intestine as part of bile.

facts.cloze: Some bilirubin is excreted in {{c1::feces}} and some in {{c2::urine}}.
facts.text: Some bilirubin is excreted in feces and some in urine.

facts.cloze: Fig 11.7: heme groups are broken down to {{c1::biliverdin}}, then bilirubin.
facts.text: Fig 11.7: heme groups are broken down to biliverdin, then bilirubin.

facts.cloze: WBCs are spherical cells with a {{c1::nucleus}}; they lack {{c2::hemoglobin}}.
facts.text: WBCs are spherical cells with a nucleus; they lack hemoglobin.

facts.cloze: WBCs are {{c1::larger}} than erythrocytes and move by {{c2::ameboid movement}}.
facts.text: WBCs are larger than erythrocytes and move by ameboid movement.

facts.cloze: WBCs fight infections and remove dead cells and debris by {{c1::phagocytosis}}.
facts.text: WBCs fight infections and remove dead cells and debris by phagocytosis.

facts.cloze: There are {{c1::five}} types of WBCs, based on appearance in stained preparations.
facts.text: There are five types of WBCs, based on appearance in stained preparations.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Granulocytes}} contain large specific granules: {{c2::neutrophils}}, {{c3::eosinophils}}, and {{c4::basophils}}.
facts.text: Granulocytes contain large specific granules: neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils.

facts.cloze: Neutrophils are the {{c1::most common}} WBC.
facts.text: Neutrophils are the most common WBC.

facts.cloze: Neutrophils stain with {{c1::both acidic and basic}} dyes.
facts.text: Neutrophils stain with both acidic and basic dyes.

facts.cloze: Neutrophils have {{c1::two- to four}}-lobed nuclei.
facts.text: Neutrophils have two- to four-lobed nuclei.

facts.cloze: Neutrophils remain in blood for {{c1::10 to 12 hours}}, then move to tissues; they are phagocytes.
facts.text: Neutrophils remain in blood for 10 to 12 hours, then move to tissues; they are phagocytes.

facts.cloze: Dead neutrophils, cell debris, and fluid make up {{c1::pus}}.
facts.text: Dead neutrophils, cell debris, and fluid make up pus.

facts.cloze: Basophils are the {{c1::least common}} WBC.
facts.text: Basophils are the least common WBC.

facts.cloze: Basophil granules stain {{c1::blue or purple}} with basic dyes.
facts.text: Basophil granules stain blue or purple with basic dyes.

facts.cloze: Basophils release {{c1::histamine}} and {{c2::heparin}}.
facts.text: Basophils release histamine and heparin.

facts.cloze: Eosinophil granules stain {{c1::bright red}} with the dye {{c2::eosin}}.
facts.text: Eosinophil granules stain bright red with the dye eosin.

facts.cloze: Eosinophils have a {{c1::two-lobed}} nucleus.
facts.text: Eosinophils have a two-lobed nucleus.

facts.cloze: Eosinophils {{c1::reduce inflammation}} and destroy certain {{c2::worm parasites}}.
facts.text: Eosinophils reduce inflammation and destroy certain worm parasites.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Agranulocytes}} have no specific granules: {{c2::lymphocytes}} and {{c3::monocytes}}.
facts.text: Agranulocytes have no specific granules: lymphocytes and monocytes.

facts.cloze: Lymphocytes have a large, {{c1::blue/purple}} stained nucleus and function in the {{c2::immune response}}.
facts.text: Lymphocytes have a large, blue/purple stained nucleus and function in the immune response.

facts.cloze: Lymphocyte types include {{c1::T cells}} and {{c2::B cells}}; they lead to production of {{c3::antibodies}}.
facts.text: Lymphocyte types include T cells and B cells; they lead to production of antibodies.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Monocytes}} are the largest WBCs.
facts.text: Monocytes are the largest WBCs.

facts.cloze: Monocytes leave the bloodstream, enter tissues, and produce {{c1::macrophages}}.
facts.text: Monocytes leave the bloodstream, enter tissues, and produce macrophages.

facts.cloze: Platelets are minute {{c1::fragments of cells}}: a little cytoplasm surrounded by a cell membrane.
facts.text: Platelets are minute fragments of cells: a little cytoplasm surrounded by a cell membrane.

facts.cloze: Platelets are produced in red bone marrow from large cells called {{c1::megakaryocytes}}.
facts.text: Platelets are produced in red bone marrow from large cells called megakaryocytes.

facts.cloze: Blood loss is minimized by {{c1::vascular spasm}}, {{c2::platelet plugs}}, and {{c3::blood clotting (coagulation)}}.
facts.text: Blood loss is minimized by vascular spasm, platelet plugs, and blood clotting (coagulation).

facts.cloze: Vascular spasm is an immediate but {{c1::temporary}} constriction of a vessel caused by contraction of {{c2::smooth muscle}} in its wall.
facts.text: Vascular spasm is an immediate but temporary constriction of a vessel caused by contraction of smooth muscle in its wall.

facts.cloze: Vascular spasm can close {{c1::small vessels}} completely and stop blood flow through them.
facts.text: Vascular spasm can close small vessels completely and stop blood flow through them.

facts.cloze: Vascular spasm is stimulated by {{c1::thromboxanes}} (released by platelets) and {{c2::endothelin}} (released by cells lining the damaged vessel).
facts.text: Vascular spasm is stimulated by thromboxanes (released by platelets) and endothelin (released by cells lining the damaged vessel).

facts.cloze: Platelet {{c1::adhesion}} occurs first: platelets stick to exposed {{c2::collagen}} in the damaged vessel wall.
facts.text: Platelet adhesion occurs first: platelets stick to exposed collagen in the damaged vessel wall.

facts.cloze: Activated platelets change shape, release chemicals that activate more platelets, and express {{c1::fibrinogen receptors}}.
facts.text: Activated platelets change shape, release chemicals that activate more platelets, and express fibrinogen receptors.

facts.cloze: In platelet {{c1::aggregation}}, {{c2::fibrinogen}} forms bridges between the fibrinogen receptors of many platelets.
facts.text: In platelet aggregation, fibrinogen forms bridges between the fibrinogen receptors of many platelets.

facts.cloze: Fig 11.10: platelet adhesion involves {{c1::von Willebrand factor}}; the platelet release reaction releases {{c2::ADP}} and thromboxane.
facts.text: Fig 11.10: platelet adhesion involves von Willebrand factor; the platelet release reaction releases ADP and thromboxane.

facts.cloze: A clot is a network of thread-like proteins called {{c1::fibrin}} that traps blood cells, platelets and fluid.
facts.text: A clot is a network of thread-like proteins called fibrin that traps blood cells, platelets and fluid.

facts.cloze: Clotting factors are proteins in {{c1::plasma}}, activated only after {{c2::injury}}.
facts.text: Clotting factors are proteins in plasma, activated only after injury.

facts.cloze: Clotting factors are made in the {{c1::liver}} and require {{c2::vitamin K}}.
facts.text: Clotting factors are made in the liver and require vitamin K.

facts.cloze: Clot step 1: injury activates clotting factors (exposed connective tissue or release of {{c1::thromboplastin}}), producing {{c2::prothrombinase}}.
facts.text: Clot step 1: injury activates clotting factors (exposed connective tissue or release of thromboplastin), producing prothrombinase.

facts.cloze: Clot step 2: {{c1::prothrombin}} is converted to its active form, {{c2::thrombin}}.
facts.text: Clot step 2: prothrombin is converted to its active form, thrombin.

facts.cloze: Clot step 3: thrombin activates {{c1::fibrinogen}} into {{c2::fibrin}}, which forms a network that traps blood.
facts.text: Clot step 3: thrombin activates fibrinogen into fibrin, which forms a network that traps blood.

facts.cloze: Fig 11.11: prothrombinase forms from active clotting factors plus {{c1::calcium}} and platelet chemicals.
facts.text: Fig 11.11: prothrombinase forms from active clotting factors plus calcium and platelet chemicals.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Anticoagulants}} prevent clots from forming, e.g. heparin, antithrombin, and warfarin (Coumadin).
facts.text: Anticoagulants prevent clots from forming, e.g. heparin, antithrombin, and warfarin (Coumadin).

facts.cloze: At an injury, enough clotting factors are activated that anticoagulants {{c1::can't work in that area}}.
facts.text: At an injury, enough clotting factors are activated that anticoagulants can't work in that area.

facts.cloze: A {{c1::thrombus}} is a clot attached to the wall of a vessel or the heart.
facts.text: A thrombus is a clot attached to the wall of a vessel or the heart.

facts.cloze: An {{c1::embolus}} is a thrombus that broke loose and floats through the circulation; it can block a vessel in the heart, lungs, or brain.
facts.text: An embolus is a thrombus that broke loose and floats through the circulation; it can block a vessel in the heart, lungs, or brain.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Clot retraction}} is condensing of the clot by actin and myosin in platelets.
facts.text: Clot retraction is condensing of the clot by actin and myosin in platelets.

facts.cloze: Clot retraction helps healing by pulling the {{c1::edges of the vessel}} closer together.
facts.text: Clot retraction helps healing by pulling the edges of the vessel closer together.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Fibrinolysis}} is the process of dissolving a clot.
facts.text: Fibrinolysis is the process of dissolving a clot.

facts.cloze: Plasminogen is activated by thrombin and {{c1::tissue plasminogen activator}} to {{c2::plasmin}}, which breaks down fibrin.
facts.text: Plasminogen is activated by thrombin and tissue plasminogen activator to plasmin, which breaks down fibrin.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Agglutination}} is clumping of blood cells in a transfusion reaction; {{c2::hemolysis}} (rupture of RBCs) can occur.
facts.text: Agglutination is clumping of blood cells in a transfusion reaction; hemolysis (rupture of RBCs) can occur.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Antigens}} are molecules on the surface of erythrocytes.
facts.text: Antigens are molecules on the surface of erythrocytes.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Antibodies}} are proteins in plasma that bind to specific antigens.
facts.text: Antibodies are proteins in plasma that bind to specific antigens.

facts.cloze: Blood groups are named according to the {{c1::antigen}} present.
facts.text: Blood groups are named according to the antigen present.

facts.cloze: Type A blood has {{c1::A}} antigens and {{c2::anti-B}} antibodies.
facts.text: Type A blood has A antigens and anti-B antibodies.

facts.cloze: Type B blood has {{c1::B}} antigens and {{c2::anti-A}} antibodies.
facts.text: Type B blood has B antigens and anti-A antibodies.

facts.cloze: Type AB blood has {{c1::both A and B}} antigens and {{c2::neither}} antibody.
facts.text: Type AB blood has both A and B antigens and neither antibody.

facts.cloze: Type O blood has {{c1::neither A nor B}} antigens and {{c2::both anti-A and anti-B}} antibodies.
facts.text: Type O blood has neither A nor B antigens and both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.

facts.cloze: The antigens on the surface of RBCs are {{c1::genetically determined}}.
facts.text: The antigens on the surface of RBCs are genetically determined.

facts.cloze: Type O is the {{c1::universal donor}} because it has no antigens.
facts.text: Type O is the universal donor because it has no antigens.

facts.cloze: Type AB is the {{c1::universal recipient}}: it can receive A, B, AB, or O blood.
facts.text: Type AB is the universal recipient: it can receive A, B, AB, or O blood.

facts.cloze: Type A can receive {{c1::A and O}}; type B can receive {{c2::B and O}}; type O can receive only {{c3::O}}.
facts.text: Type A can receive A and O; type B can receive B and O; type O can receive only O.

facts.cloze: Type O transfusion can still cause a reaction because of {{c1::other proteins}} on RBC surfaces, and because donor antibodies can react with recipient antigens.
facts.text: Type O transfusion can still cause a reaction because of other proteins on RBC surfaces, and because donor antibodies can react with recipient antigens.

facts.cloze: Fig 11.13: type A blood given to a type {{c1::B}} recipient agglutinates, because the recipient's anti-A antibodies bind the donor's A antigens.
facts.text: Fig 11.13: type A blood given to a type B recipient agglutinates, because the recipient's anti-A antibodies bind the donor's A antigens.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Rh positive}} means having Rh antigens; Rh negative means no Rh antigens.
facts.text: Rh positive means having Rh antigens; Rh negative means no Rh antigens.

facts.cloze: Anti-Rh antibodies develop only if an {{c1::Rh⁻}} person is exposed to {{c2::Rh⁺}} blood, by transfusion or from fetus to mother.
facts.text: Anti-Rh antibodies develop only if an Rh⁻ person is exposed to Rh⁺ blood, by transfusion or from fetus to mother.

facts.cloze: Rh incompatibility in pregnancy: mother {{c1::Rh⁻}}, fetus {{c2::Rh⁺}}.
facts.text: Rh incompatibility in pregnancy: mother Rh⁻, fetus Rh⁺.

facts.cloze: The mother can be exposed to Rh⁺ blood if fetal blood {{c1::leaks through the placenta}} and mixes with hers.
facts.text: The mother can be exposed to Rh⁺ blood if fetal blood leaks through the placenta and mixes with hers.

facts.cloze: The first exposure makes the mother {{c1::produce antibodies}}; any {{c2::repeated}} mixing causes a reaction.
facts.text: The first exposure makes the mother produce antibodies; any repeated mixing causes a reaction.

facts.cloze: In {{c1::hemolytic disease of the newborn}}, maternal anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta, causing agglutination and hemolysis of fetal RBCs.
facts.text: In hemolytic disease of the newborn, maternal anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta, causing agglutination and hemolysis of fetal RBCs.

facts.cloze: Hemolytic disease of the newborn can be {{c1::fatal}} to the fetus.
facts.text: Hemolytic disease of the newborn can be fatal to the fetus.

facts.cloze: HDN is prevented by treating the mother with {{c1::RhoGAM}}, which contains antibodies against Rh antigens.
facts.text: HDN is prevented by treating the mother with RhoGAM, which contains antibodies against Rh antigens.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Blood typing}} determines the ABO and Rh groups.

facts.text: Normal hematocrit: male 40–52%, female 38–48%.

facts.text: Leukemia is cancer of the red bone marrow characterized by abnormal WBCs.

facts.cloze: Differential count: neutrophils {{c1::60–70%}}, lymphocytes {{c2::20–25%}}, monocytes {{c3::3–8%}}, eosinophils {{c4::2–4%}}, basophils {{c5::0.5–1%}}.
facts.text: Differential count: neutrophils 60–70%, lymphocytes 20–25%, monocytes 3–8%, eosinophils 2–4%, basophils 0.5–1%.

facts.text: Normal platelet count: 150,000–400,000 per µL.

facts.text: Thrombocytopenia is a greatly reduced platelet count.

facts.text: Prothrombin time (time for blood to begin clotting) is normally 9 to 12 seconds.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Pulmonary}} vessels carry blood from the right ventricle through the lungs and back to the left atrium.
facts.text: Pulmonary vessels carry blood from the right ventricle through the lungs and back to the left atrium.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Systemic}} vessels carry blood from the left ventricle through all parts of the body and back to the right atrium.
facts.text: Systemic vessels carry blood from the left ventricle through all parts of the body and back to the right atrium.

facts.cloze: Circulatory system functions: carries blood; exchanges nutrients, waste, gases; transports substances; regulates {{c1::blood pressure}}; directs {{c2::blood flow}} to tissues.
facts.text: Circulatory system functions: carries blood; exchanges nutrients, waste, gases; transports substances; regulates blood pressure; directs blood flow to tissues.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Arteries}} carry blood away from the heart and are thick with a lot of elastic tissue and smooth muscle.
facts.text: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and are thick with a lot of elastic tissue and smooth muscle.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Veins}} carry blood toward the heart and have less elastic tissue and smooth muscle.
facts.text: Veins carry blood toward the heart and have less elastic tissue and smooth muscle.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Capillaries}} are where exchange occurs between blood and tissue fluids.
facts.text: Capillaries are where exchange occurs between blood and tissue fluids.

facts.cloze: Flow: heart → elastic arteries → {{c1::muscular arteries}} → {{c2::arterioles}} → capillaries → {{c3::venules}} → small veins → medium veins → large veins → heart.
facts.text: Flow: heart → elastic arteries → muscular arteries → arterioles → capillaries → venules → small veins → medium veins → large veins → heart.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::pulmonary trunk}} carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs and branches into right and left pulmonary arteries.
facts.text: The pulmonary trunk carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs and branches into right and left pulmonary arteries.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Four}} pulmonary veins exit the lungs and carry O₂-rich blood to the {{c2::left atrium}}.
facts.text: Four pulmonary veins exit the lungs and carry O₂-rich blood to the left atrium.

facts.cloze: Oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins passes LA → LV → {{c1::aorta}}.
facts.text: Oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins passes LA → LV → aorta.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::tunica intima}} is the innermost layer: simple squamous {{c2::endothelium}}.
facts.text: The tunica intima is the innermost layer: simple squamous endothelium.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::tunica media}} is the middle layer: smooth muscle with elastin and collagen fibers.
facts.text: The tunica media is the middle layer: smooth muscle with elastin and collagen fibers.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::tunica adventitia}} (tunica externa) is the outermost layer of {{c2::dense connective tissue}}.
facts.text: The tunica adventitia (tunica externa) is the outermost layer of dense connective tissue.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Elastic arteries}} are largest in diameter with the thickest walls, e.g. the {{c2::aorta and pulmonary trunk}}.
facts.text: Elastic arteries are largest in diameter with the thickest walls, e.g. the aorta and pulmonary trunk.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Muscular arteries}} are medium to small, contain smooth muscle cells, and control blood flow to body regions ({{c2::distributing arteries}}).
facts.text: Muscular arteries are medium to small, contain smooth muscle cells, and control blood flow to body regions (distributing arteries).

facts.cloze: Contraction of vessel smooth muscle is {{c1::vasoconstriction}}: diameter and blood flow {{c2::decrease}}.
facts.text: Contraction of vessel smooth muscle is vasoconstriction: diameter and blood flow decrease.

facts.cloze: Relaxation of vessel smooth muscle is {{c1::vasodilation}}: diameter and blood flow {{c2::increase}}.
facts.text: Relaxation of vessel smooth muscle is vasodilation: diameter and blood flow increase.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Arterioles}} carry blood from small arteries to capillaries; they have three thin tunics and are adapted for vasoconstriction and vasodilation.
facts.text: Arterioles carry blood from small arteries to capillaries; they have three thin tunics and are adapted for vasoconstriction and vasodilation.

facts.cloze: Fig 13.1a: in elastic arteries the tunica media is mostly {{c1::elastic connective tissue}}; elastic recoil prevents blood pressure from falling rapidly.
facts.text: Fig 13.1a: in elastic arteries the tunica media is mostly elastic connective tissue; elastic recoil prevents blood pressure from falling rapidly.

facts.cloze: Fig 13.1c: in arterioles the tunica media is only {{c1::one or two layers}} of circular smooth muscle cells.
facts.text: Fig 13.1c: in arterioles the tunica media is only one or two layers of circular smooth muscle cells.

facts.cloze: Blood flows from {{c1::arterioles}} into capillaries, which branch to form networks.
facts.text: Blood flows from arterioles into capillaries, which branch to form networks.

facts.cloze: Capillary blood flow is regulated by smooth muscle cells called {{c1::precapillary sphincters}}.
facts.text: Capillary blood flow is regulated by smooth muscle cells called precapillary sphincters.

facts.cloze: Capillary walls are just {{c1::1 layer of simple squamous epithelium}}, to facilitate diffusion.
facts.text: Capillary walls are just 1 layer of simple squamous epithelium, to facilitate diffusion.

facts.cloze: Fig 13.3: substances such as {{c1::O₂}} leave the blood in capillaries; substances such as {{c2::CO₂}} enter the blood.
facts.text: Fig 13.3: substances such as O₂ leave the blood in capillaries; substances such as CO₂ enter the blood.

facts.cloze: Blood flows from capillaries into {{c1::venules}}, then into small veins.
facts.text: Blood flows from capillaries into venules, then into small veins.

facts.cloze: All {{c1::3 tunics}} are present in small veins.
facts.text: All 3 tunics are present in small veins.

facts.cloze: Medium-sized veins collect blood from small veins and deliver it to {{c1::large veins}}.
facts.text: Medium-sized veins collect blood from small veins and deliver it to large veins.

facts.cloze: Large veins contain {{c1::valves}} to prevent backflow of blood due to gravity.
facts.text: Large veins contain valves to prevent backflow of blood due to gravity.

facts.cloze: Fig 13.1e: venules have only the {{c1::tunica intima}} resting on a delicate layer of dense connective tissue.
facts.text: Fig 13.1e: venules have only the tunica intima resting on a delicate layer of dense connective tissue.

facts.cloze: Fig 13.1g: in large veins the predominant layer is the {{c1::tunica externa}}.
facts.text: Fig 13.1g: in large veins the predominant layer is the tunica externa.

facts.cloze: Arteries distribute blood from the {{c1::aorta}} to all portions of the body.
facts.text: Arteries distribute blood from the aorta to all portions of the body.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::ascending aorta}} passes superiorly from the left ventricle.
facts.text: The ascending aorta passes superiorly from the left ventricle.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Coronary arteries}} arise from the base of the ascending aorta to serve the heart.
facts.text: Coronary arteries arise from the base of the ascending aorta to serve the heart.

facts.cloze: The aortic arch has 3 major branches: {{c1::brachiocephalic}}, {{c2::left common carotid}}, and {{c3::left subclavian}} arteries.
facts.text: The aortic arch has 3 major branches: brachiocephalic, left common carotid, and left subclavian arteries.

facts.cloze: The descending aorta has a {{c1::thoracic}} part (thorax to diaphragm) and an {{c2::abdominal}} part.
facts.text: The descending aorta has a thoracic part (thorax to diaphragm) and an abdominal part.

facts.cloze: The abdominal aorta extends from the diaphragm to where it divides into the two {{c1::common iliac arteries}}.
facts.text: The abdominal aorta extends from the diaphragm to where it divides into the two common iliac arteries.

facts.cloze: The brachiocephalic artery is the {{c1::first}} branch off the aortic arch.
facts.text: The brachiocephalic artery is the first branch off the aortic arch.

facts.cloze: The brachiocephalic artery divides into the {{c1::right common carotid}} (right head and neck) and the {{c2::right subclavian}} (right upper limb).
facts.text: The brachiocephalic artery divides into the right common carotid (right head and neck) and the right subclavian (right upper limb).

facts.cloze: The left common carotid is the {{c1::2nd}} branch off the arch and supplies the left side of the head and neck.
facts.text: The left common carotid is the 2nd branch off the arch and supplies the left side of the head and neck.

facts.cloze: The left subclavian is the {{c1::3rd}} branch off the arch and supplies the {{c2::left upper limb}}.
facts.text: The left subclavian is the 3rd branch off the arch and supplies the left upper limb.

facts.cloze: The cerebral arterial circle ({{c1::circle of Willis}}) supplies blood to most of the brain.
facts.text: The cerebral arterial circle (circle of Willis) supplies blood to most of the brain.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::internal carotid arteries}} pass into the cranial cavity.
facts.text: The internal carotid arteries pass into the cranial cavity.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Vertebral arteries}} branch from the subclavian arteries and unite to form the {{c2::basilar artery}}.
facts.text: Vertebral arteries branch from the subclavian arteries and unite to form the basilar artery.

facts.cloze: Branches of the cerebral arterial circle supply the brain and {{c1::upper spinal cord}}.
facts.text: Branches of the cerebral arterial circle supply the brain and upper spinal cord.

facts.cloze: Fig 13.8 includes the {{c1::anterior communicating}} and {{c2::posterior communicating}} arteries in the cerebral arterial circle.
facts.text: Fig 13.8 includes the anterior communicating and posterior communicating arteries in the cerebral arterial circle.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::axillary artery}} is the continuation of the subclavian in the axilla.
facts.text: The axillary artery is the continuation of the subclavian in the axilla.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::brachial artery}} continues from the axillary into the arm and is where {{c2::blood pressure}} measurements are taken.
facts.text: The brachial artery continues from the axillary into the arm and is where blood pressure measurements are taken.

facts.cloze: The ulnar and radial arteries branch from the brachial artery at the {{c1::elbow}}.
facts.text: The ulnar and radial arteries branch from the brachial artery at the elbow.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::radial artery}} is on the thumb side and is used to take the {{c2::pulse}}.
facts.text: The radial artery is on the thumb side and is used to take the pulse.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::celiac trunk}} supplies the stomach, pancreas, spleen, liver, and upper duodenum.
facts.text: The celiac trunk supplies the stomach, pancreas, spleen, liver, and upper duodenum.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::superior mesenteric artery}} supplies the small intestine and upper portion of the colon.
facts.text: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the small intestine and upper portion of the colon.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::inferior mesenteric artery}} supplies the colon.
facts.text: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the colon.

facts.cloze: The celiac trunk, SMA and IMA are {{c1::unpaired visceral}} branches of the abdominal aorta.
facts.text: The celiac trunk, SMA and IMA are unpaired visceral branches of the abdominal aorta.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Renal arteries}} supply the kidneys; {{c2::suprarenal arteries}} supply the adrenal glands.
facts.text: Renal arteries supply the kidneys; suprarenal arteries supply the adrenal glands.

facts.cloze: Gonadal arteries are the {{c1::testicular}} arteries (testes) and {{c2::ovarian}} arteries (ovaries).
facts.text: Gonadal arteries are the testicular arteries (testes) and ovarian arteries (ovaries).

facts.cloze: Parietal branches of the abdominal aorta: {{c1::inferior phrenic}} arteries (diaphragm) and {{c2::lumbar}} arteries (lumbar vertebrae and back muscles).
facts.text: Parietal branches of the abdominal aorta: inferior phrenic arteries (diaphragm) and lumbar arteries (lumbar vertebrae and back muscles).

facts.cloze: In the systemic circulation, blood returning to the heart in veins is {{c1::deoxygenated}}.
facts.text: In the systemic circulation, blood returning to the heart in veins is deoxygenated.

facts.cloze: In the pulmonary circulation, blood returning to the heart in the pulmonary veins is {{c1::oxygenated}}.
facts.text: In the pulmonary circulation, blood returning to the heart in the pulmonary veins is oxygenated.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::superior vena cava}} returns blood from the head, neck, thorax, and right upper limbs.
facts.text: The superior vena cava returns blood from the head, neck, thorax, and right upper limbs.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::inferior vena cava}} returns blood from the abdomen, pelvis, and lower limbs.
facts.text: The inferior vena cava returns blood from the abdomen, pelvis, and lower limbs.

facts.cloze: Both venae cavae empty into the {{c1::right atrium}}.
facts.text: Both venae cavae empty into the right atrium.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::external jugular vein}} drains the head and neck and empties into the subclavian vein.
facts.text: The external jugular vein drains the head and neck and empties into the subclavian vein.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::internal jugular vein}} drains the brain, face and neck and empties into the subclavian vein.
facts.text: The internal jugular vein drains the brain, face and neck and empties into the subclavian vein.

facts.cloze: Subclavian veins form the {{c1::brachiocephalic veins}}.
facts.text: Subclavian veins form the brachiocephalic veins.

facts.cloze: Brachiocephalic veins join to form the {{c1::superior vena cava}}.
facts.text: Brachiocephalic veins join to form the superior vena cava.

facts.cloze: Deep veins of the upper limb follow the arteries and have the {{c1::same names}} as the arteries.
facts.text: Deep veins of the upper limb follow the arteries and have the same names as the arteries.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::brachial vein}} empties into the axillary vein.
facts.text: The brachial vein empties into the axillary vein.

facts.cloze: Superficial veins empty into {{c1::deep veins}}.
facts.text: Superficial veins empty into deep veins.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Cephalic veins}} empty into the axillary vein and basilic vein.
facts.text: Cephalic veins empty into the axillary vein and basilic vein.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::median cubital vein}} connects to the cephalic vein near the elbow and is used for {{c2::drawing blood}}.
facts.text: The median cubital vein connects to the cephalic vein near the elbow and is used for drawing blood.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::liver}} is a major processing center for substances absorbed by the intestinal tract.
facts.text: The liver is a major processing center for substances absorbed by the intestinal tract.

facts.cloze: A {{c1::portal system}} begins with capillaries in the viscera and ends with capillaries in the liver.
facts.text: A portal system begins with capillaries in the viscera and ends with capillaries in the liver.

facts.cloze: The hepatic portal system uses the {{c1::splenic vein}} and {{c2::superior mesenteric vein}}.
facts.text: The hepatic portal system uses the splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein.

facts.cloze: After processing, {{c1::hepatic veins}} leave the liver and empty into the {{c2::inferior vena cava}}.
facts.text: After processing, hepatic veins leave the liver and empty into the inferior vena cava.

facts.cloze: Fig 13.15 also labels the {{c1::inferior mesenteric vein}} and gastric veins draining into this system.
facts.text: Fig 13.15 also labels the inferior mesenteric vein and gastric veins draining into this system.

facts.cloze: Blood pressure is the force blood exerts against {{c1::blood vessel walls}}, caused by the heart's rhythmic contractions.
facts.text: Blood pressure is the force blood exerts against blood vessel walls, caused by the heart's rhythmic contractions.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Systolic}} pressure is during contraction of the heart; {{c2::diastolic}} pressure is during relaxation.
facts.text: Systolic pressure is during contraction of the heart; diastolic pressure is during relaxation.

facts.cloze: Average blood pressure is {{c1::120/80}} (systolic/diastolic).
facts.text: Average blood pressure is 120/80 (systolic/diastolic).

facts.cloze: Fig 13.17: BP is measured with a pressure cuff on the arm; the sounds heard are {{c1::Korotkoff sounds}}.
facts.text: Fig 13.17: BP is measured with a pressure cuff on the arm; the sounds heard are Korotkoff sounds.

facts.cloze: Fig 13.17: systolic pressure is where sound is {{c1::first heard}}; diastolic is where sound {{c2::disappears}}.
facts.text: Fig 13.17: systolic pressure is where sound is first heard; diastolic is where sound disappears.

facts.cloze: As blood flows from arteries through capillaries and veins, pressure falls progressively to about {{c1::zero}} as it enters the right atrium.
facts.text: As blood flows from arteries through capillaries and veins, pressure falls progressively to about zero as it enters the right atrium.

facts.cloze: The difference between systolic and diastolic pressure gets {{c1::smaller}} as blood moves into smaller-diameter vessels.
facts.text: The difference between systolic and diastolic pressure gets smaller as blood moves into smaller-diameter vessels.

facts.cloze: The smaller the vessel diameter, the {{c1::higher}} the resistance to blood flow.
facts.text: The smaller the vessel diameter, the higher the resistance to blood flow.

facts.cloze: Veins have larger diameters and therefore {{c1::lower}} resistance.
facts.text: Veins have larger diameters and therefore lower resistance.

facts.cloze: Blood keeps flowing toward the heart in veins because of {{c1::valves}} and {{c2::skeletal muscle contractions}} that compress veins.
facts.text: Blood keeps flowing toward the heart in veins because of valves and skeletal muscle contractions that compress veins.

facts.cloze: Muscular arteries, arterioles, and {{c1::precapillary sphincters}} can vasoconstrict and vasodilate to control blood flow into regions and tissues.
facts.text: Muscular arteries, arterioles, and precapillary sphincters can vasoconstrict and vasodilate to control blood flow into regions and tissues.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Pulse pressure}} is the difference between systolic and diastolic pressure; 120/80 gives {{c2::40 mmHg}}.
facts.text: Pulse pressure is the difference between systolic and diastolic pressure; 120/80 gives 40 mmHg.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Stroke volume}} and {{c2::vascular compliance}} affect pulse pressure.
facts.text: Stroke volume and vascular compliance affect pulse pressure.

facts.cloze: Vascular compliance is related to the {{c1::elasticity}} of the blood vessel wall.
facts.text: Vascular compliance is related to the elasticity of the blood vessel wall.

facts.cloze: Ejection of blood into the aorta creates a pressure wave, the {{c1::pulse}}, felt near large arteries.
facts.text: Ejection of blood into the aorta creates a pressure wave, the pulse, felt near large arteries.

facts.cloze: Most exchange across capillary walls occurs by {{c1::diffusion}}.
facts.text: Most exchange across capillary walls occurs by diffusion.

facts.cloze: Blood pressure, capillary {{c1::permeability}}, and {{c2::osmosis}} affect fluid movement across capillary walls.
facts.text: Blood pressure, capillary permeability, and osmosis affect fluid movement across capillary walls.

facts.cloze: Blood pressure forces fluid {{c1::out of}} capillaries; osmosis moves fluid {{c2::into}} capillaries.
facts.text: Blood pressure forces fluid out of capillaries; osmosis moves fluid into capillaries.

facts.cloze: Fluid moves into capillaries by osmosis because blood has a greater {{c1::osmotic pressure}} than interstitial fluid.
facts.text: Fluid moves into capillaries by osmosis because blood has a greater osmotic pressure than interstitial fluid.

facts.cloze: There is a net movement of fluid from blood into {{c1::tissues}}; this fluid is removed by the {{c2::lymphatic system}}.
facts.text: There is a net movement of fluid from blood into tissues; this fluid is removed by the lymphatic system.

facts.cloze: Fig 13.20: at the {{c1::arterial}} end, blood pressure is greater than osmotic pressure, so fluid moves out into the interstitial space.
facts.text: Fig 13.20: at the arterial end, blood pressure is greater than osmotic pressure, so fluid moves out into the interstitial space.

facts.cloze: Fig 13.20: at the {{c1::venous}} end, osmotic pressure is greater than blood pressure, so fluid moves into the capillary.
facts.text: Fig 13.20: at the venous end, osmotic pressure is greater than blood pressure, so fluid moves into the capillary.

facts.cloze: Fig 13.20: about {{c1::1/10}} of the volume goes to the lymphatic capillaries.
facts.text: Fig 13.20: about 1/10 of the volume goes to the lymphatic capillaries.

facts.cloze: Local control of blood flow is achieved by relaxation and contraction of {{c1::precapillary sphincters}}.
facts.text: Local control of blood flow is achieved by relaxation and contraction of precapillary sphincters.

facts.cloze: When precapillary sphincters relax, blood flow {{c1::increases}}.
facts.text: When precapillary sphincters relax, blood flow increases.

facts.cloze: Precapillary sphincters are controlled by the {{c1::metabolic needs}} of tissues; nutrient concentration also controls blood flow.
facts.text: Precapillary sphincters are controlled by the metabolic needs of tissues; nutrient concentration also controls blood flow.

facts.cloze: Blood flow increases when {{c1::oxygen}} levels decrease.
facts.text: Blood flow increases when oxygen levels decrease.

facts.cloze: {{c1::New capillaries}} can grow into an area if its metabolic activity increases often.
facts.text: New capillaries can grow into an area if its metabolic activity increases often.

facts.cloze: The {{c1::vasomotor center}} (in the pons and medulla oblongata, per V70) works through the {{c2::sympathetic}} division and controls vessel diameter.
facts.text: The vasomotor center (in the pons and medulla oblongata, per V70) works through the sympathetic division and controls vessel diameter.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Vasomotor tone}} is a state of partial constriction of blood vessels.
facts.text: Vasomotor tone is a state of partial constriction of blood vessels.

facts.cloze: An increase in vasomotor tone makes blood vessels {{c1::constrict}} and blood pressure go {{c2::up}}.
facts.text: An increase in vasomotor tone makes blood vessels constrict and blood pressure go up.

facts.cloze: Hormonal control: the sympathetic division releases {{c1::epinephrine and norepinephrine}} from the adrenal medulla.
facts.text: Hormonal control: the sympathetic division releases epinephrine and norepinephrine from the adrenal medulla.

facts.cloze: In most vessels epinephrine and norepinephrine cause {{c1::constriction}}; in skeletal and cardiac muscle they cause {{c2::dilation}}.
facts.text: In most vessels epinephrine and norepinephrine cause constriction; in skeletal and cardiac muscle they cause dilation.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Mean arterial pressure}} (MAP) is a calculated value reflecting average arterial pressure in the body's vessels.
facts.text: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is a calculated value reflecting average arterial pressure in the body's vessels.

facts.cloze: MAP equals cardiac output times peripheral resistance: {{c1::MAP = CO × PR}}.
facts.text: MAP equals cardiac output times peripheral resistance: MAP = CO × PR.

facts.cloze: Cardiac output equals {{c1::heart rate}} times {{c2::stroke volume}}.
facts.text: Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume.

facts.cloze: {{c1::Peripheral resistance}} is the resistance to blood flow in all the blood vessels.
facts.text: Peripheral resistance is the resistance to blood flow in all the blood vessels.

facts.cloze: MAP changes in response to changes in {{c1::HR, SV, or PR}}.
facts.text: MAP changes in response to changes in HR, SV, or PR.

facts.cloze: MAP is about {{c1::70 mmHg}} at birth.
facts.text: MAP is about 70 mmHg at birth.

facts.cloze: MAP is about {{c1::95 mmHg}} from adolescence to middle age and may reach {{c2::110 mmHg}} in a healthy older person.
facts.text: MAP is about 95 mmHg from adolescence to middle age and may reach 110 mmHg in a healthy older person.

facts.cloze: Baroreceptor reflexes activate responses to keep blood pressure in the {{c1::normal range}}.
facts.text: Baroreceptor reflexes activate responses to keep blood pressure in the normal range.

facts.cloze: Baroreceptors respond to {{c1::stretch}} in arteries due to increased pressure.
facts.text: Baroreceptors respond to stretch in arteries due to increased pressure.

facts.cloze: For BP regulation, baroreceptors are located in the {{c1::carotid sinuses}} and {{c2::aortic arch}}.
facts.text: For BP regulation, baroreceptors are located in the carotid sinuses and aortic arch.

facts.cloze: Baroreceptor reflexes change {{c1::peripheral resistance}}, heart rate, and stroke volume.
facts.text: Baroreceptor reflexes change peripheral resistance, heart rate, and stroke volume.

facts.cloze: Fig 13.23: parasympathetic stimulation through the {{c1::vagus nerve}} decreases heart rate.
facts.text: Fig 13.23: parasympathetic stimulation through the vagus nerve decreases heart rate.

facts.cloze: Fig 13.23: sympathetic stimulation {{c1::increases}} HR and SV and makes blood vessels {{c2::constrict}}.
facts.text: Fig 13.23: sympathetic stimulation increases HR and SV and makes blood vessels constrict.

facts.cloze: Fig 13.24: when BP rises, the cardioregulatory center increases {{c1::parasympathetic}} and decreases {{c2::sympathetic}} stimulation; HR and SV decrease and blood vessels {{c3::dilate}}.
facts.text: Fig 13.24: when BP rises, the cardioregulatory center increases parasympathetic and decreases sympathetic stimulation; HR and SV decrease and blood vessels dilate.

facts.cloze: Chemoreceptors are sensitive to changes in blood {{c1::oxygen}}, {{c2::carbon dioxide}}, and {{c3::pH}}.
facts.text: Chemoreceptors are sensitive to changes in blood oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH.

facts.cloze: Chemoreceptors are located in the {{c1::carotid bodies}} and {{c2::aortic bodies}}, near the carotid sinuses and aortic arch.
facts.text: Chemoreceptors are located in the carotid bodies and aortic bodies, near the carotid sinuses and aortic arch.
