recall.q: What three components make up the cardiovascular system?
recall.a: Heart, blood vessels, and blood.

recall.q: Which side of the heart drives the pulmonary circulation, and where does that blood return?
recall.a: The right side; blood goes to the lungs and returns to the left side of the heart.

recall.q: About how much blood does a resting adult heart pump per minute?
recall.a: Approximately 5 L per minute.

recall.q: List the four functions of the heart.
recall.a: Generates blood pressure; routes blood between pulmonary and systemic circulations; ensures one-way blood flow; regulates blood supply.

recall.q: Where is the apex of the heart?
recall.a: Behind the 5th and 6th ribs at the 5th intercostal space, left of the sternum.

recall.q: In which body region does the heart sit?
recall.a: The mediastinum of the thoracic cavity.

recall.q: Which pericardial layer lines the fibrous pericardium?
recall.a: The parietal pericardium.

recall.q: What fills the pericardial cavity, and what does it do?
recall.a: A thin layer of pericardial fluid that reduces friction as the heart moves.

recall.q: Why is cardiac tamponade dangerous?
recall.a: Fluid/blood in the pericardial cavity compresses the heart and interrupts pumping; a person can die quickly if it is not removed.

recall.q: What other name does Fig 12.4 give the visceral pericardium?
recall.a: Epicardium.

recall.q: Trace blood from the venae cavae to the aorta.
recall.a: RA → tricuspid valve → RV → pulmonary semilunar valve → pulmonary trunk → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → LA → bicuspid valve → LV → aortic semilunar valve → aorta.

recall.q: Which valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle?
recall.a: The bicuspid valve.

recall.q: Which vessels bring blood from the lungs to the heart?
recall.a: The pulmonary veins (to the left atrium).

recall.q: Where does coronary venous blood drain, per Fig 12.10?
recall.a: Through the coronary sinus/cardiac veins into the right atrium.

recall.q: What connects cardiac muscle cells physically and electrically?
recall.a: Intercalated disks with gap junctions.

recall.q: In what direction do action potentials spread across the ventricular wall?
recall.a: From the apex toward the base.

recall.q: Name the 5 steps of Fig 12.14.
recall.a: Heart at rest → atria stimulated → atria contract → ventricles stimulated → ventricles contract.

recall.q: Which channels open during the depolarization phase?
recall.a: Voltage-gated Na⁺ and voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels.

recall.q: What prolongs the cardiac action potential?
recall.a: The plateau phase, by keeping Ca²⁺ channels open.

recall.q: Why can't cardiac muscle undergo tetanic contraction?
recall.a: Its refractory period lets it relax almost completely before another action potential.

recall.q: Compare the duration of skeletal and cardiac action potentials.
recall.a: Skeletal ≈ 2 msec; cardiac ≈ 200–500 msec.

recall.q: Give the 5-step action potential path through the heart.
recall.a: SA node → AV node → AV bundle → right & left bundle branches → Purkinje fibers.

recall.q: Why is conduction through the AV node slow?
recall.a: So the atria can complete their contraction before action potentials reach the ventricles.

recall.q: What is an ectopic beat?
recall.a: An action potential that originates outside the SA node; it may cause fibrillation.

recall.q: Where is the SA node and what is its role?
recall.a: In the right atrium; it is where the action potential originates (pacemaker).

recall.q: What does the P wave represent?
recall.a: Depolarization of the atria (leads to atrial contraction).

recall.q: Which ECG event also leads to atrial relaxation?
recall.a: The QRS complex (ventricular depolarization).

recall.q: What does the T wave represent?
recall.a: Repolarization of the ventricles (leads to ventricular relaxation).

recall.q: Give the state of the valves when the heart is completely relaxed.
recall.a: AV valves open, SL valves closed; ventricles fill passively.

recall.q: What closes the AV valves at the start of ventricular systole?
recall.a: Blood pushed back as the ventricles begin to contract from the apex upward.

recall.q: What closes the SL valves?
recall.a: As the ventricles relax, pressure falls and draws blood backwards against the SL valves.

recall.q: What are the roles of the atria versus the ventricles?
recall.a: Atria are primers for the pumps; ventricles are the actual pumps.

recall.q: What causes the first heart sound?
recall.a: Closure of the atrioventricular valves (lubb).

recall.q: What causes the second heart sound?
recall.a: Closure of the semilunar valves (dupp).

recall.q: What causes murmurs?
recall.a: Incompetent or stenosed valves.

recall.q: Write the cardiac output formula and typical values.
recall.a: CO = SV × HR; SV ≈ 70 mL/beat, HR ≈ 72 beats/min, CO ≈ 5 L/min.

recall.q: Define preload.
recall.a: The degree the ventricular walls are stretched at the end of diastole.

recall.q: Define afterload.
recall.a: The pressure against which the ventricles must pump blood.

recall.q: State Starling's law of the heart.
recall.a: Relationship between preload and SV: more venous return → more stretch → greater force → ↑ SV and CO.

recall.q: Where are the baroreceptors that regulate heart function (Heart deck)?
recall.a: In the aorta and internal carotid arteries.

recall.q: What happens to autonomic output to the heart when BP falls?
recall.a: Sympathetic stimulation increases and parasympathetic stimulation decreases; HR, SV and CO rise.

recall.q: What do chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata respond to?
recall.a: Changes in pH and CO₂.

recall.q: How does body temperature affect heart rate?
recall.a: Higher temperature increases HR; lower temperature decreases HR.

recall.q: What is coronary artery disease?
recall.a: Narrowing of the coronary arteries, which decreases blood supply to the heart.

recall.q: What causes a myocardial infarction?
recall.a: Closure of one or more coronary arteries.

recall.q: What is an infarct?
recall.a: The scar left where cardiac muscle lacking adequate blood supply died.

recall.q: Distinguish angioplasty, stent and bypass.
recall.a: Angioplasty opens blocked vessels; a stent keeps vessels open; bypass reroutes blood away from blocked arteries.

recall.q: How much does cardiac output fall by age 70?
recall.a: By one-third.

recall.q: Why does the left ventricle hypertrophy with age?
recall.a: Increased afterload.

recall.q: Give the composition of plasma.
recall.a: 91% water, 7% proteins, 2% other; plasma is 55% of blood volume.

recall.q: Which plasma protein maintains water balance, and what % is it?
recall.a: Albumin, 58% of plasma proteins.

recall.q: How does serum differ from plasma?
recall.a: Serum is plasma without the clotting factors.

recall.q: Which formed element is most abundant?
recall.a: RBCs, almost 95% of all formed elements.

recall.q: Where does hematopoiesis occur before and after birth?
recall.a: Fetus: liver, thymus, spleen, lymph nodes, red bone marrow. After birth: mainly red bone marrow (some WBCs in lymphatic tissues).

recall.q: What are the two stem cell lines and what does each produce?
recall.a: Myeloid → most formed elements; lymphoid → lymphocytes.

recall.q: What is another name for hematopoietic stem cells?
recall.a: Hemocytoblasts.

recall.q: Why can't mature RBCs divide?
recall.a: They lose their nuclei and most organelles during development.

recall.q: How many iron atoms are in each heme, and what binds to it?
recall.a: One iron atom; O₂ binds to the iron (oxyhemoglobin).

recall.q: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous to O₂ transport?
recall.a: It binds hemoglobin more readily than O₂.

recall.q: Give the three ways CO₂ is transported, with percentages.
recall.a: 70% as bicarbonate ions, 23% bound to globin, 7% dissolved in plasma.

recall.q: Outline how low blood O₂ increases RBC production.
recall.a: Kidneys ↑ erythropoietin → red bone marrow ↑ RBC production → blood O₂ rises (negative feedback).

recall.q: What nutrients does RBC production depend on?
recall.a: Sufficient iron and several B vitamins.

recall.q: What happens to globin, iron and heme from old RBCs?
recall.a: Globin → amino acids; iron is recycled; heme → bilirubin.

recall.q: Where does bilirubin go?
recall.a: Taken up by the liver, released into the small intestine in bile; excreted in feces and some in urine.

recall.q: Name the three granulocytes and two agranulocytes.
recall.a: Granulocytes: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils. Agranulocytes: lymphocytes, monocytes.

recall.q: Which WBC is most common, and what does it form at infection sites?
recall.a: Neutrophil; dead neutrophils + debris + fluid = pus.

recall.q: Which WBC releases histamine and heparin?
recall.a: Basophil.

recall.q: Which WBC destroys worm parasites?
recall.a: Eosinophil.

recall.q: Which WBC becomes macrophages?
recall.a: Monocyte (largest WBC).

recall.q: Name the three processes that minimize blood loss.
recall.a: Vascular spasm, platelet plug formation, and blood clotting (coagulation).

recall.q: What two chemicals stimulate vascular spasm, and where does each come from?
recall.a: Thromboxanes from platelets; endothelin from cells lining the damaged vessel.

recall.q: Give the 3 steps of platelet plug formation.
recall.a: Adhesion to exposed collagen → activation (shape change, chemical release, fibrinogen receptors) → aggregation via fibrinogen bridges.

recall.q: Give the three steps of clot formation.
recall.a: Prothrombinase production → thrombin production (prothrombin → thrombin) → fibrin production (fibrinogen → fibrin).

recall.q: Where are clotting factors made and what vitamin do they need?
recall.a: In the liver; they require vitamin K.

recall.q: Distinguish a thrombus from an embolus.
recall.a: Thrombus = clot attached to a vessel or heart wall; embolus = thrombus that broke loose and floats in the circulation.

recall.q: How is a clot dissolved?
recall.a: Fibrinolysis: thrombin and tissue plasminogen activator turn plasminogen into plasmin, which breaks down fibrin.

recall.q: List the antigens and antibodies for types A, B, AB, O.
recall.a: A: A antigen, anti-B. B: B antigen, anti-A. AB: both antigens, no antibodies. O: no antigens, anti-A and anti-B.

recall.q: Why is type O the universal donor?
recall.a: Its RBCs have no A or B antigens.

recall.q: Which blood can a type B patient receive?
recall.a: B and O.

recall.q: Why can type O blood still cause a reaction?
recall.a: Other proteins on RBC surfaces, and donor antibodies can react with the recipient's RBC antigens.

recall.q: When do anti-Rh antibodies form?
recall.a: Only after an Rh⁻ person is exposed to Rh⁺ blood (transfusion or from fetus).

recall.q: Why is the first Rh⁺ pregnancy of an Rh⁻ mother usually the sensitizing one?
recall.a: The first exposure makes her produce antibodies; repeated mixing causes the reaction.

recall.q: How is HDN prevented?
recall.a: Treating the mother with RhoGAM (antibodies against Rh antigens).

recall.q: Define hematocrit and give the normal ranges.
recall.a: % of blood volume that is RBCs; male 40–52%, female 38–48%.

recall.q: What does a crossmatch test?
recall.a: Donor cells + recipient serum, and donor serum + recipient cells.

recall.q: Give the normal WBC differential percentages.
recall.a: Neutrophils 60–70, lymphocytes 20–25, monocytes 3–8, eosinophils 2–4, basophils 0.5–1 (%).

recall.q: Define leukopenia, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia.
recall.a: Low WBC count; high WBC count; greatly reduced platelet count.

recall.q: Which ABO type is most common in both US groups on the slide?
recall.a: Type O (47% and 46%).

recall.q: Which ABO type is least common in both groups?
recall.a: Type AB (3% and 7%).

recall.q: In which group is type B more common: Caucasians or African-Americans?
recall.a: African-Americans (20% vs 9%).

recall.q: Define arteries, veins and capillaries by function.
recall.a: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins toward the heart; capillaries are the site of exchange.

recall.q: Give the sequence of vessels from the heart and back.
recall.a: Elastic arteries → muscular arteries → arterioles → capillaries → venules → small veins → medium veins → large veins → heart.

recall.q: What does the pulmonary trunk carry, and how many pulmonary veins are there?
recall.a: Deoxygenated blood from the RV to the lungs; four pulmonary veins carry O₂-rich blood to the LA.

recall.q: Name the three tunics from inside out with their tissue.
recall.a: Intima (simple squamous endothelium), media (smooth muscle + elastin + collagen), adventitia/externa (dense connective tissue).

recall.q: Distinguish elastic from muscular arteries.
recall.a: Elastic: largest, thickest walls (aorta, pulmonary trunk). Muscular: medium–small, smooth muscle, distribute blood to regions.

recall.q: What do vasoconstriction and vasodilation do to diameter and flow?
recall.a: Vasoconstriction decreases both; vasodilation increases both.

recall.q: What regulates blood flow into capillaries?
recall.a: Precapillary sphincters (smooth muscle cells).

recall.q: Why is the capillary wall a single layer of simple squamous epithelium?
recall.a: To facilitate diffusion between capillaries and surrounding cells.

recall.q: Which veins contain valves and why?
recall.a: Large veins, to prevent backflow of blood due to gravity.

recall.q: Name the three aortic arch branches in order.
recall.a: Brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian.

recall.q: What two arteries come from the brachiocephalic artery?
recall.a: Right common carotid and right subclavian.

recall.q: Where do the coronary arteries arise?
recall.a: From the base of the ascending aorta.

recall.q: Where does the abdominal aorta end?
recall.a: Where it divides into the two common iliac arteries.

recall.q: Which arteries feed the cerebral arterial circle?
recall.a: The internal carotid arteries and the basilar artery (from the two vertebral arteries).

recall.q: Where is blood pressure measured, and where is the pulse taken?
recall.a: BP at the brachial artery; pulse at the radial artery (thumb side).

recall.q: Give the upper-limb artery sequence.
recall.a: Subclavian → axillary → brachial → radial and ulnar (at the elbow).

recall.q: What does the celiac trunk supply?
recall.a: Stomach, pancreas, spleen, liver, upper duodenum.

recall.q: Name the paired visceral branches of the abdominal aorta.
recall.a: Renal, suprarenal, and gonadal (testicular/ovarian) arteries.

recall.q: Distinguish the SMA from the IMA.
recall.a: SMA: small intestine and upper colon. IMA: colon.

recall.q: What does the SVC drain?
recall.a: Head, neck, thorax, and right upper limbs.

recall.q: What does the IVC drain?
recall.a: Abdomen, pelvis, and lower limbs.

recall.q: In which circulation do veins carry oxygenated blood?
recall.a: Pulmonary circulation (pulmonary veins).

recall.q: Trace blood from the internal jugular vein to the heart.
recall.a: Internal jugular → subclavian → brachiocephalic → superior vena cava → right atrium.

recall.q: Which upper-limb vein is used to draw blood?
recall.a: The median cubital vein, near the elbow.

recall.q: How are deep upper-limb veins named?
recall.a: They follow the arteries and have the same names.

recall.q: What makes the hepatic portal system a 'portal' system?
recall.a: It begins with capillaries in the viscera and ends with capillaries in the liver.

recall.q: Which two veins does the hepatic portal system use (per the slide)?
recall.a: Splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein.

recall.q: Where does blood go after the liver?
recall.a: Hepatic veins → inferior vena cava → right atrium.

recall.q: Define pulse pressure and calculate it for 120/80.
recall.a: Systolic − diastolic; 120 − 80 = 40 mmHg.

recall.q: How does vessel diameter affect resistance?
recall.a: Smaller diameter → higher resistance.

recall.q: Why does blood still return in low-resistance, low-pressure veins?
recall.a: Valves prevent backflow and skeletal muscle contractions compress veins.

recall.q: What happens to BP from arteries to the right atrium?
recall.a: It falls progressively to about zero.

recall.q: What happens at the arterial end of a capillary?
recall.a: Blood pressure > osmotic pressure → net fluid movement out into the interstitial space.

recall.q: What happens at the venous end?
recall.a: Osmotic pressure > blood pressure → net fluid movement into the capillary.

recall.q: What removes the fluid that does not return to the capillary?
recall.a: The lymphatic system.

recall.q: What happens to local blood flow when tissue O₂ falls?
recall.a: Blood flow increases (precapillary sphincters relax).

recall.q: Define vasomotor tone and the effect of increasing it.
recall.a: Partial constriction of vessels; increasing it constricts vessels and raises BP.

recall.q: How do epinephrine and norepinephrine affect vessels in skeletal and cardiac muscle?
recall.a: They cause dilation (most other vessels constrict).

recall.q: Write the MAP formula and the CO formula.
recall.a: MAP = CO × PR; CO = HR × SV.

recall.q: What three variables change MAP?
recall.a: Heart rate, stroke volume, and peripheral resistance.

recall.q: Give MAP at birth, adulthood, and older age.
recall.a: ≈70 mmHg at birth; ≈95 mmHg adolescence to middle age; up to 110 mmHg in healthy older people.

recall.q: Where are baroreceptors and what do they sense (Vessels deck)?
recall.a: Carotid sinuses and aortic arch; they sense stretch from increased pressure.

recall.q: What three variables do baroreceptor reflexes change?
recall.a: Peripheral resistance, heart rate, stroke volume.

recall.q: Where are chemoreceptors and what do they sense?
recall.a: Carotid and aortic bodies; blood O₂, CO₂, and pH.

recall.q: What does the adrenal medulla secrete in this mechanism?
recall.a: Epinephrine and norepinephrine.

recall.q: Where do these hormones cause vasodilation instead of vasoconstriction?
recall.a: In skeletal and cardiac muscle.

recall.q: What triggers the mechanism (Fig 13.26)?
recall.a: Increased stimulation from physical activity or stress.

recall.q: Give the RAAS sequence.
recall.a: ↓ blood flow → kidney renin → angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → (ACE) → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone → kidneys conserve Na⁺ and water.

recall.q: What are the two effects of angiotensin II?
recall.a: Vasoconstriction, and stimulating the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone.

recall.q: What does aldosterone do?
recall.a: Makes the kidneys conserve sodium and water, so less water is lost in urine and BP is maintained.

recall.q: What triggers ADH release, and from where?
recall.a: Increased plasma solute concentration or decreased BP; hypothalamic nerve cells.

recall.q: What does ADH do to urine volume?
recall.a: Kidneys absorb more water, so urine volume decreases.

recall.q: Where does ANH come from and what does it do?
recall.a: Right atrium (when atrial BP rises); kidneys lose Na⁺ and water → ↑ urine, ↓ blood volume, ↓ BP.

recall.q: Which mechanism is most important for short-term BP regulation?
recall.a: Baroreceptor reflexes.

recall.q: Name the three long-term BP mechanisms.
recall.a: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, antidiuretic hormone, atrial natriuretic hormone.

recall.q: How do long-term mechanisms differ from short-term?
recall.a: They respond to small changes and act gradually; short-term react quickly to sudden changes.

recall.q: Distinguish arteriosclerosis from atherosclerosis.
recall.a: Arteriosclerosis = arteries less elastic; atherosclerosis = a type of it caused by plaque deposits in artery walls.

recall.q: List the factors that contribute to atherosclerosis.
recall.a: Lack of exercise, smoking, obesity, diet high in cholesterol and trans fats, some genetics.

recall.q: What is plaque?
recall.a: Deposits of material in artery walls (atherosclerosis).

recall.q: Trace the arteries from the external iliac to the foot.
recall.a: External iliac → femoral → popliteal → anterior tibial (→ dorsalis pedis) / posterior tibial (→ fibular).

recall.q: What do the superior phrenic arteries supply?
recall.a: The diaphragm.

recall.q: What do the internal iliac arteries supply?
recall.a: The pelvic area (visceral and parietal branches).

recall.q: Where do the posterior intercostal veins drain on each side?
recall.a: Right: azygos vein. Left: hemiazygos or accessory hemiazygos vein.

recall.q: Distinguish the great and small saphenous veins.
recall.a: Great: dorsal and medial foot. Small: lateral foot, joins the popliteal vein.

recall.q: Where do the common iliac veins empty?
recall.a: Into the inferior vena cava.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly describes the two circulations?
options: The right side pumps blood to all body tissues (systemic circulation).
Both sides pump blood only to the lungs.
The right side pumps blood to the lungs and back to the left side (pulmonary circulation).
The left side pumps blood to the lungs and back to the right side.
quiz.explanation: H5: the right side → lungs → left side is the pulmonary circulation; the left side → all other tissues → right side is the systemic circulation.

quiz.stem: The cardiovascular system consists of:
options: The heart, blood vessels, and blood
quiz.explanation: H3 lists the heart, blood vessels, and blood as the members of the cardiovascular system.

quiz.stem: A student is asked to locate the apex of the heart on a classmate. Based on the slides, where should they palpate?
options: 5th intercostal space, left of the sternum
Directly behind the sternum at the 2nd intercostal space
5th intercostal space, right of the sternum
2nd intercostal space, right of the sternum
quiz.explanation: H8: the apex is behind the 5th and 6th ribs at the 5th intercostal space to the left of the sternum.

quiz.stem: All of the following are functions of the heart, EXCEPT:
options: Routing blood between the pulmonary and systemic circulations
quiz.explanation: H7 lists the 4 heart functions. Erythropoietin is made by the kidneys (B16).

quiz.stem: After chest trauma, a patient has blood collecting in the pericardial cavity that compresses the heart and interrupts its pumping. Which condition best explains this?
quiz.explanation: H10: cardiac tamponade = fluid or blood in the pericardial cavity compressing the heart from the outside.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches a pericardial layer with its description?
options: Visceral pericardium — lines the fibrous pericardium
Fibrous pericardium — membrane on the heart's surface
Serous pericardium — outer layer of tough connective tissue
Parietal pericardium — lines the fibrous pericardium
quiz.explanation: H9: parietal lines the fibrous pericardium; visceral is on the heart's surface; the fibrous layer is the tough outer layer.

quiz.stem: Pericardial fluid is found between which two layers?
options: Visceral pericardium and the heart muscle
quiz.explanation: H9: the pericardial cavity is the space between the parietal and visceral pericardia.

quiz.stem: Pericarditis is inflammation of the:
quiz.explanation: H10: pericarditis is inflammation of the serous pericardium.

quiz.stem: Which sequence correctly traces blood from the right atrium to the lungs?
options: Right atrium → bicuspid valve → right ventricle → aortic semilunar valve → aorta
Right atrium → pulmonary semilunar valve → right ventricle → pulmonary veins
Right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary semilunar valve → pulmonary trunk
Right atrium → tricuspid valve → left ventricle → pulmonary trunk
quiz.explanation: Fig 12.10 (H12) flow chart: RA → tricuspid → RV → pulmonary semilunar valve → pulmonary trunk → pulmonary arteries → lung tissue.

quiz.stem: Oxygenated blood returning from the lungs enters which chamber first?
quiz.explanation: H12 and V19: the pulmonary veins carry O₂-rich blood to the left atrium.

quiz.stem: As blood leaves the left ventricle it passes through the:
quiz.explanation: Fig 12.10 (H12): left ventricle → aortic semilunar valve → aorta.

quiz.stem: According to Fig 12.10, blood that has supplied the heart tissue returns to the heart through the:
options: Pulmonary veins, into the left atrium
Inferior vena cava, into the left ventricle
Coronary sinus and cardiac veins, into the right atrium
quiz.explanation: H12 flow chart: aorta → coronary arteries → heart tissue → coronary sinus/cardiac veins → right atrium.

quiz.stem: Which feature lets cardiac muscle cells act together both physically and electrically?
quiz.explanation: H13: intercalated disks with gap junctions connect cells both physically and electrically.

quiz.stem: Which description best fits cardiac muscle cells?
options: Unbranched cells that do not use Ca²⁺
Non-striated spindle cells with few mitochondria
One central nucleus, branching, striated, rich in mitochondria
quiz.explanation: H13 lists: one centrally located nucleus, branching, rich in mitochondria, striated.

quiz.stem: During ventricular stimulation, action potentials spread across the ventricular wall:
options: From the apex toward the base
From the base toward the apex
From the right atrium to the left atrium
quiz.explanation: H17 step 4: action potentials spread across the ventricular wall from the apex toward the base.

quiz.stem: During the plateau phase of a cardiac muscle action potential:
options: Na⁺ channels close, some K⁺ channels open, and Ca²⁺ channels remain open
K⁺ channels close and Ca²⁺ channels close
Na⁺ channels open widely and Ca²⁺ channels close
quiz.explanation: H19: plateau = Na⁺ channels close, some K⁺ channels open, Ca²⁺ channels remain open.

quiz.stem: Which statement best explains why cardiac muscle does not undergo tetanic contractions?
options: Its long action potential and refractory period let it relax almost completely before the next action potential
quiz.explanation: H20: the refractory period allows nearly complete relaxation and prevents tetanic, sustained contractions.

quiz.stem: Which ion channels open during the depolarization phase of a cardiac muscle action potential?
options: Na⁺ channels close and K⁺ channels open
quiz.explanation: H19: depolarization = voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes skeletal from cardiac muscle action potentials?
options: Skeletal lasts 200–500 msec; cardiac lasts about 2 msec
Cardiac action potentials have no repolarization phase
Skeletal lasts about 2 msec; cardiac lasts 200–500 msec
quiz.explanation: H20: skeletal muscle action potentials take 2 msec; cardiac take 200 to 500 msec.

quiz.stem: During the repolarization phase:
options: Ca²⁺ channels open and K⁺ channels close
K⁺ channels are open and Ca²⁺ channels close
quiz.explanation: H20: repolarization = K⁺ channels open, Ca²⁺ channels close.

quiz.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the path of an action potential through the heart?
options: Purkinje fibers → bundle branches → AV bundle → AV node → SA node
AV node → SA node → bundle branches → AV bundle → Purkinje fibers
SA node → AV bundle → AV node → Purkinje fibers → bundle branches
SA node → AV node → AV bundle → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers
quiz.explanation: H27 lists the path: SA node, AV node, AV bundle, right and left bundle branches, Purkinje fibers.

quiz.stem: Which statement best explains the slow conduction through the AV node?
options: It lets the ventricles contract before the atria
It lets the atria complete contraction before the ventricles are stimulated
It speeds delivery of action potentials to the apex
It stops ectopic beats from forming
quiz.explanation: H24: the slow rate allows the atria to complete their contraction before action potentials reach the ventricles.

quiz.stem: An ECG shows beats that start somewhere other than the SA node. Based on the slides, these are called:
options: Purkinje beats, which slow the heart
Ectopic beats, which may cause fibrillation
quiz.explanation: H23: action potentials originating in another area of the heart are ectopic beats, which may cause fibrillation.

quiz.stem: The SA node is located in the:
quiz.explanation: H23: SA node — in RA.

quiz.stem: Which structures carry action potentials down the interventricular septum to the apex?
quiz.explanation: H25: the AV bundle divides into left and right bundle branches that travel down the interventricular septum to the apex.

quiz.stem: The heart's pacemaker contains a large number of which channels?
quiz.explanation: H23: the SA node has a large number of Ca²⁺ channels.

quiz.stem: Which ECG component represents ventricular depolarization?
quiz.explanation: H30: QRS complex = depolarization of the ventricles.

quiz.stem: Per the slides, which ECG event leads to ventricular contraction AND atrial relaxation?
quiz.explanation: H30: the QRS complex leads to ventricular contraction and atrial relaxation.

quiz.stem: The T wave represents:
options: Ventricular repolarization, leading to ventricular relaxation
quiz.explanation: H30: T wave = repolarization of the ventricles; leads to ventricular relaxation.

quiz.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
quiz.explanation: H30: P = atrial depolarization; QRS = ventricular depolarization; T = ventricular repolarization.

quiz.stem: When the heart is completely relaxed:
options: AV valves are open, SL valves are closed, and the ventricles fill passively
AV valves are closed and SL valves are open
Blood is ejected into the aorta
quiz.explanation: H35 step 1: AV valves open, SL valves closed; passive filling of ventricles.

quiz.stem: Which best explains the closing of the AV valves at the start of ventricular systole?
options: Blood in the aorta flows back into the ventricles
The atria contract and pull the valves shut
The SL valves close first and force them shut
Ventricles contract from the apex upward and blood pushes the AV valves closed
quiz.explanation: H35 step 3: as the ventricles begin to contract from the apex upward, blood closes the AV valves.

quiz.stem: Blood moves through the heart chambers because:
options: Gravity pulls blood through the chambers
Contractions create pressure changes, and blood moves from high to low pressure
Blood moves from low to high pressure
quiz.explanation: H33: pressure changes are responsible for blood movement; blood moves from high to low pressure.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes the roles of the chambers?
options: The ventricles are primers; the atria are the actual pumps
The atria are primers; the ventricles are the actual pumps
Only the right side of the heart pumps
Atria and ventricles contract at the same time
quiz.explanation: H32: the atria are primers for the pumps and the ventricles are the actual pumps.

quiz.stem: During ventricular diastole, the SL valves close because:
options: Blood enters the atria and raises pressure
The ventricles contract from the apex
Ventricular pressure falls, drawing blood backward against the valves
quiz.explanation: H35 step 5: as the ventricles relax, pressure decreases, drawing blood backwards to close the SL valves.

quiz.stem: In Fig 12.19, left ventricular volume at the end of diastole is about:
quiz.explanation: H37 (Fig 12.19, panel 3): end-diastolic volume sits at the 125 mL mark; end-systolic at 55 mL.

quiz.stem: On auscultation a patient has an abnormal heart sound. Per the slides, murmurs are due to:
options: Ectopic beats in the SA node
quiz.explanation: H38: abnormal heart sounds are called murmurs and are due to incompetent or stenosed valves.

quiz.stem: The first heart sound ('lubb') is caused by:
quiz.explanation: H38: the first heart sound is due to closure of the atrioventricular valves.

quiz.stem: The second heart sound ('dupp') is caused by:
quiz.explanation: H38: the second heart sound is due to closure of the semilunar valves.

quiz.stem: A person has a stroke volume of 70 mL/beat and a heart rate of 72 beats/min. Their cardiac output is closest to:
quiz.explanation: CO = SV × HR (H40) = 70 × 72 = 5040 mL/min ≈ 5 L/min. Values from H41.

quiz.stem: If HR = 80 beats/min and SV = 60 mL/beat, cardiac output is:
quiz.explanation: CO = SV × HR (H40) = 60 × 80 = 4800 mL/min = 4.8 L/min.

quiz.stem: During exercise venous return increases. According to Starling's law, which follows?
options: Heart rate falls to keep CO constant
Greater stretch of the ventricles → stronger contraction → increased SV and CO
quiz.explanation: H43: increased venous return stretches the fibers, which contract with greater force, increasing SV and CO; exercise is the slide's example.

quiz.stem: Afterload is best defined as:
options: The stretch of the ventricles at the end of diastole
The amount of blood returning to the heart
The pressure against which the ventricles must pump blood
The number of beats per minute
quiz.explanation: H43: afterload = pressure against which ventricles must pump blood.

quiz.stem: Preload is:
options: The degree the ventricular walls are stretched at the end of diastole
The resistance of all blood vessels
quiz.explanation: H42: preload = degree ventricular walls are stretched at end of diastole.

quiz.stem: A patient has long-standing high blood pressure. Which best explains the extra work for the ventricles?
options: Higher afterload means a greater force of contraction is needed to open the SL valves
quiz.explanation: H43: high blood pressure means a greater force of ventricular contraction is needed to open the SL valves (afterload).

quiz.stem: Intrinsic regulation of the heart:
options: Is controlled within the heart itself and does not depend on neural or hormonal regulation
Depends on epinephrine from the adrenal medulla
Depends on the sympathetic nervous system
quiz.explanation: H42: intrinsic regulation = mechanisms contained within the heart itself; does not depend on neural or hormonal regulation.

quiz.stem: A patient loses blood and BP drops. Which baroreceptor reflex response follows?
options: The SA node stops firing until BP recovers
Parasympathetic stimulation increases and cardiac output falls
Less baroreceptor stimulation → ↑ sympathetic, ↓ parasympathetic → ↑ HR, SV and CO
quiz.explanation: H45–H46: BP decrease → less baroreceptor stimulation → increased sympathetic and decreased parasympathetic stimulation → HR, SV, CO increase.

quiz.stem: In the Heart deck, baroreceptors are described as monitoring blood pressure in the:
quiz.explanation: H45: baroreceptors monitor blood pressure in the aorta and internal carotid arteries.

quiz.stem: The cardioregulatory center is located in the:
quiz.explanation: H45: action potentials go to the cardioregulatory center in the medulla oblongata.

quiz.stem: Parasympathetic stimulation of the heart:
options: Has no effect on the SA node
Releases epinephrine from the adrenal medulla
Decreases heart rate and stroke volume
Increases heart rate and stroke volume
quiz.explanation: H44: parasympathetic nerves decrease heart rate and stroke volume.

quiz.stem: A patient retains CO₂ and blood pH falls. Per Fig 12.22, which response follows?
options: Medullary chemoreceptors detect the pH drop and control centers increase stimulation of the heart, raising HR and SV
Parasympathetic stimulation increases and SV falls
Baroreceptors in the aorta lower heart rate
quiz.explanation: H49–H50: medulla chemoreceptors detect decreased pH (often from increased CO₂); control centers increase stimulation of the heart and adrenal medulla; HR and SV increase.

quiz.stem: Per the slides, which would decrease heart rate?
quiz.explanation: H48: lower temperature decreases heart rate; elevated temperature, epinephrine and excitement increase it (H48–H49).

quiz.stem: All of the following can increase cardiac output, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: H49: excitement, anxiety, anger and epinephrine can increase cardiac output; depression can decrease it.

quiz.stem: In Fig 12.23, parasympathetic fibers reach the heart through the:
quiz.explanation: H51 (Fig 12.23) labels 'Parasympathetic nerve fibers — Vagus nerves' and 'Sympathetic nerve fibers — Cardiac nerves'.

quiz.stem: A patient has closure of a coronary artery, and part of the heart muscle dies and scars. This is best described as:
quiz.explanation: H52: MI is due to closure of one or more coronary arteries; muscle lacking blood supply dies and scars (infarct).

quiz.stem: Coronary artery disease:
options: Decreases blood supply to the heart because coronary arteries are narrowed
Is inflammation of the serous pericardium
Increases blood supply to the heart
quiz.explanation: H52: CAD decreases blood supply to the heart; coronary arteries are narrowed.

quiz.stem: Which procedure reroutes blood away from blocked arteries?
quiz.explanation: H54: bypass reroutes blood away from blocked arteries.

quiz.stem: Which is an effect of aging on the heart, per the slides?
options: Cardiac output decreases by one-third by age 70
quiz.explanation: H55: cardiac output decreases by one-third by age 70; arrhythmias increase; LV hypertrophies; exercise helps at any age.

quiz.stem: Plasma makes up about what percent of total blood volume?
quiz.explanation: B4: plasma is 55% of total blood volume; formed elements are 45%.

quiz.stem: Which plasma protein is most abundant and helps maintain water balance?
quiz.explanation: B6: albumin is 58% of plasma proteins and helps maintain water balance.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes serum from plasma?
options: Serum is plasma with extra fibrinogen
Serum is plasma without the clotting factors
quiz.explanation: B6: serum is plasma without the clotting factors.

quiz.stem: A blood sample is centrifuged. The bottom red layer is about 45% of the tube. This layer is the:
quiz.explanation: B4–B5 (Fig 11.1): formed elements are 45% of total blood; plasma is 55%.

quiz.stem: Globulins make up about what % of plasma proteins, and what do they do?
options: 38%; help the immune system and act as transport molecules
quiz.explanation: B6: globulins are 38% of plasma proteins; they help the immune system and act as transport molecules.

quiz.stem: Which formed element makes up almost 95% of all formed elements?
quiz.explanation: B7: RBCs make up almost 95% of all formed elements.

quiz.stem: All of the following are functions of blood, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: B3 lists blood's functions. Generating blood pressure is a function of the heart (H7).

quiz.stem: After birth, hematopoiesis is confined primarily to the:
quiz.explanation: B8: after birth hematopoiesis is confined primarily to red bone marrow.

quiz.stem: Which stem cell gives rise to lymphocytes?
quiz.explanation: B9: lymphoid stem cells give rise to lymphocytes.

quiz.stem: Platelets come from which cell, per Fig 11.2?
quiz.explanation: B10 (Fig 11.2): myeloid stem cell → megakaryocyte → platelets; B29 confirms megakaryocytes.

quiz.stem: In the fetus, hematopoiesis occurs in all of the following, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: B8: fetal sites are liver, thymus, spleen, lymph nodes, and red bone marrow.

quiz.stem: Which feature of RBCs explains why they cannot divide?
options: They lose their nuclei and most organelles during development
quiz.explanation: B11: RBCs lose their nuclei and most organelles during development and are unable to undergo cell division.

quiz.stem: A person found in a closed garage with a running car engine has poor O₂ delivery. Which best explains this?
options: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin more readily than O₂
Carbon monoxide converts heme to bilirubin
quiz.explanation: B13: carbon monoxide can bind to hemoglobin more readily than O₂.

quiz.stem: How long do RBCs live?
quiz.explanation: B11: RBCs live for about 110–120 days.

quiz.stem: Each heme group contains:
quiz.explanation: B13: each heme contains one iron atom.

quiz.stem: Most CO₂ in the blood is transported as:
quiz.explanation: B15: about 70% of CO₂ is transported as bicarbonate ions.

quiz.stem: Which enzyme in RBCs converts CO₂ and water into H⁺ and bicarbonate?
quiz.explanation: B15: the reaction in RBCs uses the enzyme carbonic anhydrase.

quiz.stem: About 23% of CO₂ is transported:
options: Bound to the globin protein of hemoglobin
quiz.explanation: B15: about 23% of CO₂ is bound to the globin protein of hemoglobin.

quiz.stem: A person moves to a high altitude where blood O₂ falls. Which sequence best explains the rise in RBC count?
options: Liver ↑ bilirubin → spleen ↑ RBCs → O₂ rises
Red bone marrow ↑ erythropoietin → kidneys ↑ RBCs
Kidneys ↑ erythropoietin → red bone marrow ↑ RBC production → blood O₂ rises
quiz.explanation: B16 and Fig 11.6 (B18): decreased O₂ → kidneys increase erythropoietin → red bone marrow produces more RBCs → increased O₂; negative feedback.

quiz.stem: Erythropoietin is produced by the:
quiz.explanation: B16: decreased blood O₂ causes the kidneys to increase production of erythropoietin.

quiz.stem: RBC production depends on sufficient:
quiz.explanation: B16: the process depends on having sufficient iron and several B vitamins.

quiz.stem: Which pair correctly matches a part of hemoglobin with its fate?
options: Globin — broken down into amino acids
quiz.explanation: B19: globin → amino acids; iron is recycled; heme → bilirubin.

quiz.stem: After heme is converted to bilirubin, the bilirubin is:
options: Taken up by the liver and released into the small intestine as part of bile
quiz.explanation: B19: bilirubin is taken up by the liver and released into the small intestine as part of bile.

quiz.stem: Old RBCs are removed from the blood by:
options: Macrophages in the spleen and liver
quiz.explanation: B19: old RBCs are removed by macrophages in the spleen and liver.

quiz.stem: In Fig 11.5, which stage comes just before a mature red blood cell?
quiz.explanation: B17 (Fig 11.5): late erythroblast → reticulocyte → red blood cell.

quiz.stem: A smear shows the most common WBC, with a 2–4-lobed nucleus, staining with both acidic and basic dyes. Which cell is it?
quiz.explanation: B23: neutrophils are most common, stain with both acidic and basic dyes, and have two to four lobed nuclei.

quiz.stem: A patient has a worm parasite infection. Which WBC destroys certain worm parasites and reduces inflammation?
quiz.explanation: B25: eosinophils reduce inflammation and destroy certain worm parasites.

quiz.stem: Which WBC releases histamine and heparin?
quiz.explanation: B25: basophils release histamine and heparin.

quiz.stem: Which WBC is the largest and produces macrophages?
quiz.explanation: B27: monocytes are the largest WBCs; they leave the blood, enter tissues and produce macrophages.

quiz.stem: Which pair of cells are agranulocytes?
quiz.explanation: B27: agranulocytes (no specific granules) = lymphocytes and monocytes.

quiz.stem: Pus at a site of infection is made of:
options: Dead neutrophils, cell debris, and fluid
quiz.explanation: B23: dead neutrophils, cell debris, and fluid make up pus.

quiz.stem: T cells and B cells are types of:
quiz.explanation: B27: lymphocytes — several different types (T cells and B cells).

quiz.stem: Which WBC is the least common?
quiz.explanation: B25: basophils are the least common.

quiz.stem: Which sequence correctly describes platelet plug formation?
options: Adhesion to collagen → activation and release of chemicals → aggregation by fibrinogen bridges
quiz.explanation: B32–B33: platelet adhesion occurs first, then activation, then aggregation as fibrinogen bridges fibrinogen receptors.

quiz.stem: Vascular spasm is stimulated by:
options: Thromboxanes from platelets and endothelin from cells lining the damaged vessel
quiz.explanation: B31: thromboxanes (platelets) and endothelin (cells lining the damaged vessel).

quiz.stem: Activated platelets express surface receptors called:
quiz.explanation: B32: activated platelets express fibrinogen receptors.

quiz.stem: When a vessel is damaged, blood loss is minimized by which three processes?
options: Vascular spasm, platelet plugs, and coagulation
quiz.explanation: B30: vascular spasm, platelet plugs, and blood clotting (coagulation).

quiz.stem: Platelets are best described as:
options: Cell fragments produced from megakaryocytes in red bone marrow
Plasma proteins made in the liver
quiz.explanation: B29: platelets are minute fragments of cells, produced in red bone marrow from megakaryocytes.

quiz.stem: Which sequence correctly describes clot formation?
options: Fibrin production → thrombin production → prothrombinase production
Thrombin production → prothrombinase production → fibrinogen production
Plasmin production → thrombin production → fibrin breakdown
Prothrombinase production → thrombin production → fibrin production
quiz.explanation: B36: 1) prothrombinase production, 2) thrombin production, 3) fibrin production.

quiz.stem: A patient with liver disease and vitamin K deficiency bleeds easily. Which best explains this?
options: Platelets are made in the liver
Clotting factors are made in the liver and require vitamin K
Vitamin K forms the fibrin network directly
quiz.explanation: B35: clotting factors are made in the liver and require vitamin K.

quiz.stem: Thrombin converts:
quiz.explanation: B36: thrombin activates fibrinogen into its active form, fibrin.

quiz.stem: Per Fig 11.11, what combines with active clotting factors to form prothrombinase?
quiz.explanation: B37 (Fig 11.11): active clotting factors + calcium and platelet chemicals → prothrombinase.

quiz.stem: A clot breaks loose from a leg vein and travels to the lungs. This traveling clot is a(n):
quiz.explanation: B38: an embolus is a thrombus that broke loose and floats through the circulation; it can block a vessel in the heart, lungs, or brain.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as an anticoagulant on the slides?
quiz.explanation: B38 lists heparin, antithrombin, and warfarin. Thromboxane is released by platelets and stimulates vascular spasm (B31).

quiz.stem: In fibrinolysis, plasminogen is activated to plasmin by:
quiz.explanation: B39: plasminogen is activated by thrombin and tissue plasminogen activator to plasmin.

quiz.stem: Clot retraction is caused by:
options: Actin and myosin in the platelets
quiz.explanation: B39: clot retraction = condensing of the clot by actin and myosin in the platelets.

quiz.stem: A type A patient needs a transfusion. Which donor types are compatible, per the slides?
quiz.explanation: B46: type A can receive A and O blood.

quiz.stem: Type O plasma contains:
quiz.explanation: B42: type O blood plasma has both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.

quiz.stem: Type AB blood has:
options: Both A and B antigens and neither antibody
quiz.explanation: B41–B42: AB has both antigens; its plasma has neither antibody.

quiz.stem: Type A blood is given by mistake to a type B recipient. What happens, and why?
options: Agglutination, because the recipient's anti-A antibodies bind the donor's A antigens
Agglutination, because the donor's B antigens bind anti-B
No reaction, because type B has no antibodies
No reaction, because type A is a universal donor
quiz.explanation: B45 (Fig 11.13b): anti-A antibodies in the type B recipient combine with type A antigens on the donated RBCs → agglutination.

quiz.stem: Why is type O called the universal donor?
options: It is the most common blood type
Its RBCs have no A or B antigens
quiz.explanation: B46: type O are universal donors because they have no antigens.

quiz.stem: A type O unit is given to a type A patient but a reaction still occurs. Which best explains this?
options: Type A patients have anti-O antibodies
Type O RBCs carry A antigens
Other proteins on RBC surfaces, and donor antibodies reacting with the recipient's RBC antigens
quiz.explanation: B46: transfusion with type O can still cause a reaction because of other RBC surface proteins, and donor antibodies can react with recipient antigens.

quiz.stem: Antibodies are:
options: Molecules on the surface of erythrocytes
Clotting factors made in the liver
Proteins in plasma that bind to specific antigens
quiz.explanation: B40: antibodies are proteins in plasma that bind to specific antigens; antigens are on the RBC surface.

quiz.stem: An Rh⁻ mother, untreated in her first Rh⁺ pregnancy, is now pregnant with a second Rh⁺ fetus. Which best explains the risk?
options: Rh antigens from the mother cross into the fetus
There is no risk because antibodies never cross the placenta
The fetus makes anti-Rh antibodies against the mother
Anti-Rh antibodies she made after the first exposure cross the placenta and hemolyze fetal RBCs
quiz.explanation: B48–B49: the first exposure makes the mother produce antibodies; in HDN, maternal anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta and cause agglutination and hemolysis of fetal RBCs.

quiz.stem: Hemolytic disease of the newborn is prevented by giving the mother:
quiz.explanation: B49: prevented if the mother is treated with RhoGAM, which contains antibodies against Rh antigens.

quiz.stem: Anti-Rh antibodies develop only when:
options: An Rh⁻ person is exposed to Rh⁺ blood
A person receives type AB blood
An Rh⁺ person is exposed to Rh⁻ blood
quiz.explanation: B47: antibodies only develop if an Rh⁻ person is exposed to Rh⁺ blood by transfusion or from mother to fetus.

quiz.stem: Rh positive means:
quiz.explanation: B47: Rh positive means you have Rh antigens.

quiz.stem: A female's hemoglobin is 13 g/100 mL. Based on the slides, this is:
quiz.explanation: B53: normal for females is 12–16 g/100 mL.

quiz.stem: A patient's WBC count is 15,000 per µL. This is called:
quiz.explanation: B54: normal 5000–9000/µL; higher than normal = leukocytosis.

quiz.stem: Hematocrit is:
options: The % of total blood volume composed of RBCs
The number of WBCs per µL
The grams of hemoglobin per 100 mL
The time for blood to clot
quiz.explanation: B51: hematocrit = % of total blood volume composed of RBC.

quiz.stem: A crossmatch involves:
options: Timing how long blood takes to clot
Counting each of the 5 kinds of WBCs
Mixing donor cells with recipient serum, and donor serum with recipient cells
quiz.explanation: B51: crossmatch — donor's blood cells mixed with recipient's serum and donor's serum mixed with recipient's blood cells.

quiz.stem: The normal prothrombin time is:
quiz.explanation: B56: prothrombin time = time for blood to begin clotting (9 to 12 sec).

quiz.stem: A greatly reduced platelet count is called:
quiz.explanation: B56: thrombocytopenia is greatly reduced platelet count.

quiz.stem: In a normal differential count, which cell has the highest percentage?
quiz.explanation: B55: neutrophils 60–70% is the largest share.

quiz.stem: A male has a hematocrit of 45%. Based on the slides, this is:
quiz.explanation: B51: normal male hematocrit is 40–52%.

quiz.stem: According to the slide, the most common ABO type among US Caucasians is:
quiz.explanation: B43: type O, 47%; type A, 41%; type B, 9%; type AB, 3%.

quiz.stem: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs?
quiz.explanation: V19: pulmonary trunk carries deoxygenated blood from right ventricle towards lung.

quiz.stem: Pulmonary veins carry:
options: O₂-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium
Blood from the left ventricle to the aorta
Blood from the body to the right atrium
quiz.explanation: V19: four pulmonary veins exit the lungs and carry O₂-rich blood to the left atrium.

quiz.stem: Which sequence correctly describes blood flow from the heart to the capillaries?
options: Elastic arteries → muscular arteries → arterioles → capillaries
Arterioles → muscular arteries → elastic arteries → capillaries
quiz.explanation: V7: heart → elastic arteries → muscular arteries → arterioles → capillaries.

quiz.stem: Exchange between blood and tissue fluids occurs in the:
quiz.explanation: V6: capillaries — exchange occurs between blood and tissue fluids.

quiz.stem: Systemic vessels carry blood:
options: From the right atrium to the left atrium
From the left ventricle through the body and back to the right atrium
From the right ventricle through the lungs and back to the left atrium
quiz.explanation: V3: systemic vessels — from the left ventricle through all parts of the body and back to the right atrium.

quiz.stem: Which vessel layer is made of simple squamous endothelium?
quiz.explanation: V8: tunica intima — innermost layer, simple squamous (endothelium).

quiz.stem: The tunica adventitia is made of:
quiz.explanation: V8: tunica adventitia (externa) — outermost layer, dense connective tissue.

quiz.stem: Which arteries are called distributing arteries because they control blood flow to body regions?
quiz.explanation: V10: muscular arteries can control blood flow to body regions — distributing arteries.

quiz.stem: Which are examples of elastic arteries?
quiz.explanation: V10: elastic arteries — e.g. aorta and pulmonary trunk.

quiz.stem: The smooth muscle in an arteriole wall relaxes. What happens?
options: Vasodilation: vessel diameter and blood flow increase
quiz.explanation: V11: relaxation of the smooth muscle = vasodilation, which increases vessel diameter and blood flow.

quiz.stem: Arterioles are best described as vessels that:
options: Carry blood from small arteries to capillaries and are adapted for vasoconstriction and vasodilation
Are the largest arteries in the body
quiz.explanation: V11: arterioles transport blood from small arteries to capillaries; three tunics, much thinner; adapted for vasoconstriction and vasodilation.

quiz.stem: Blood flow into capillary networks is regulated by:
quiz.explanation: V13: blood flow is regulated by smooth muscle cells called precapillary sphincters.

quiz.stem: Why are capillary walls only one layer of simple squamous epithelium?
options: To facilitate diffusion between capillaries and surrounding cells
quiz.explanation: V13: walls are just 1 layer of simple squamous epithelium to facilitate diffusion.

quiz.stem: Per the slide, which veins contain valves to prevent backflow due to gravity?
quiz.explanation: V16: large veins contain valves to prevent backflow of blood due to gravity.

quiz.stem: According to Fig 13.1, venules consist of:
options: Only the tunica intima on a delicate layer of dense connective tissue
All three tunics with a thick media
quiz.explanation: V17 (Fig 13.1e): venules — only the tunica intima resting on a delicate layer of dense connective tissue.

quiz.stem: Which order of aortic arch branches is correct?
options: Left common carotid → brachiocephalic → left subclavian
Right common carotid → right subclavian → left common carotid
Left subclavian → left common carotid → brachiocephalic
Brachiocephalic → left common carotid → left subclavian
quiz.explanation: V25–V26: brachiocephalic = 1st, left common carotid = 2nd, left subclavian = 3rd branch off the aortic arch.

quiz.stem: The coronary arteries arise from the:
quiz.explanation: V22: coronary arteries arise from the base of the ascending aorta to serve the heart.

quiz.stem: The brachiocephalic artery branches into the:
options: Right common carotid and right subclavian arteries
Left common carotid and left subclavian arteries
quiz.explanation: V25: brachiocephalic → right common carotid + right subclavian.

quiz.stem: The abdominal aorta ends by dividing into the:
quiz.explanation: V23: the abdominal aorta extends from the diaphragm to where it divides into the two common iliac arteries.

quiz.stem: Which artery supplies the left upper limb?
quiz.explanation: V26: left subclavian artery — 3rd branch off aortic arch; supplies left upper limb.

quiz.stem: The thoracic aorta is the part of the descending aorta that extends:
options: Through the thorax to the diaphragm
From the diaphragm to the common iliacs
quiz.explanation: V23: thoracic — part of descending aorta that extends through thorax to diaphragm.

quiz.stem: A nurse takes a patient's pulse at the wrist on the thumb side. Which artery is used?
quiz.explanation: V31: radial is on the thumb side and used to take the pulse.

quiz.stem: Blood pressure measurements are taken at which artery?
quiz.explanation: V31: brachial arteries — where blood pressure measurements are taken.

quiz.stem: The basilar artery is formed by:
options: The union of the two vertebral arteries
quiz.explanation: V29: vertebral arteries enter the cranial cavity and unite to form the basilar artery.

quiz.stem: The axillary artery is the continuation of the:
quiz.explanation: V31: axillary arteries — continuation of subclavian in the axilla.

quiz.stem: Which artery supplies the stomach, pancreas, spleen, liver, and upper duodenum?
quiz.explanation: V35: celiac trunk artery supplies those organs.

quiz.stem: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the:
options: Small intestine and upper portion of the colon
quiz.explanation: V35: SMA supplies small intestines and upper portion of colon.

quiz.stem: Which is a paired visceral branch of the abdominal aorta?
quiz.explanation: V35–V36: celiac, SMA and IMA are unpaired; renal, suprarenal and gonadal are paired.

quiz.stem: The superior vena cava returns blood from all of the following, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: V44: SVC — head, neck, thorax, right upper limbs; IVC — abdomen, pelvis, lower limbs.

quiz.stem: Both venae cavae empty into the:
quiz.explanation: V44: both empty into the right atrium of the heart.

quiz.stem: In which circulation is the blood returning to the heart in veins oxygenated?
quiz.explanation: V43: in the pulmonary circulation, blood returning in the pulmonary veins is oxygenated.

quiz.stem: A MedTech student draws blood from a vein near the elbow. Per the slides, which vein is used for drawing blood?
quiz.explanation: V49: median cubital veins — near elbow, used for drawing blood.

quiz.stem: Which sequence describes venous drainage from the brain to the heart?
options: Subclavian → internal jugular → superior vena cava → brachiocephalic
External jugular → axillary → brachial → inferior vena cava
Internal jugular → brachiocephalic → subclavian → inferior vena cava
Internal jugular → subclavian → brachiocephalic → superior vena cava
quiz.explanation: V46–V47: internal jugular empties into subclavian; subclavian veins form brachiocephalic veins, which join to form the SVC.

quiz.stem: The brachiocephalic veins join to form the:
quiz.explanation: V47: brachiocephalic veins join to form superior vena cava.

quiz.stem: The hepatic portal system:
options: Drains directly into the superior vena cava
Carries oxygenated blood from the lungs
Begins in the liver and ends in the kidneys
Begins with capillaries in the viscera and ends with capillaries in the liver
quiz.explanation: V56: portal system — vascular system that begins with capillaries in viscera and ends with capillaries in liver.

quiz.stem: Per the slide, the hepatic portal system uses the:
options: Splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein
quiz.explanation: V56: uses splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein.

quiz.stem: After processing in the liver, blood leaves through the:
options: Hepatic veins, which empty into the inferior vena cava
Hepatic portal vein, into the aorta
quiz.explanation: V56: hepatic veins leave the liver and empty into the IVC, which returns blood to the right atrium.

quiz.stem: A patient's BP is 140/90 mmHg. Their pulse pressure is:
quiz.explanation: V65: pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic = 140 − 90 = 50 mmHg.

quiz.stem: A patient's BP is 110/70 mmHg. Their pulse pressure is:
As blood flows from the arteries through the capillaries and veins, blood pressure:
options: Falls progressively to about zero at the right atrium
quiz.explanation: V62: blood pressure falls progressively to about zero as blood enters the right atrium.

quiz.stem: Which statement about resistance is correct?
options: The smaller the vessel diameter, the higher the resistance
Resistance does not depend on diameter
quiz.explanation: V62: the smaller the diameter, the higher the resistance.

quiz.stem: Veins have low pressure and low resistance, yet blood keeps flowing toward the heart because of:
options: Elastic recoil of the tunica intima
Valves and skeletal muscle contractions compressing veins
quiz.explanation: V63: veins have valves to prevent backflow, and skeletal muscle contractions compress veins.

quiz.stem: Pulse pressure is affected by:
quiz.explanation: V65: stroke volume and vascular compliance affect pulse pressure.

quiz.stem: During manual BP measurement (Fig 13.17), the pressure at which sound is FIRST heard is the:
quiz.explanation: V61 (Fig 13.17): 'Sound is first heard' marks systolic pressure (120 mmHg); 'sound disappears' marks diastolic (80 mmHg).

quiz.stem: Vascular compliance is related to:
options: The elasticity of the blood vessel wall
The thickness of the endothelium only
quiz.explanation: V65: vascular compliance is related to the elasticity of the blood vessel wall.

quiz.stem: At the arterial end of a capillary:
options: Blood pressure exceeds osmotic pressure, so fluid moves out of the capillary
Osmotic pressure exceeds blood pressure, so fluid moves in
Fluid enters the lymphatic capillaries directly from the artery
quiz.explanation: V67 (Fig 13.20): at the arterial end, blood pressure is greater than osmotic pressure; net movement of fluid is out of the capillary.

quiz.stem: Fluid that accumulates in tissues after capillary exchange is removed by the:
quiz.explanation: V66: fluid gained in tissues is removed by the lymphatic system.

quiz.stem: Fluid moves back into the capillary at the venous end because:
options: Blood has a greater osmotic pressure than interstitial fluid, and blood pressure there is lower
quiz.explanation: V66–V67: osmosis moves fluid into capillaries because blood has greater osmotic pressure; at the venous end osmotic pressure exceeds blood pressure.

quiz.stem: Most exchange across capillary walls occurs by:
quiz.explanation: V66: most exchange across capillary walls occurs by diffusion.

quiz.stem: During exercise, O₂ levels in a muscle fall. What local response follows?
options: Vasomotor tone falls to zero everywhere
Precapillary sphincters relax and blood flow increases
Precapillary sphincters contract and flow decreases
quiz.explanation: V68: blood flow increases when O₂ decreases; sphincters relax → blood flow increases.

quiz.stem: Vasomotor tone is:
options: A state of partial constriction of blood vessels; an increase raises BP
The pressure in the right atrium
The rhythm of the SA node
quiz.explanation: V70: vasomotor tone — state of partial constriction; increase causes constriction and BP to go up.

quiz.stem: During a stress response, epinephrine has which effect on blood vessels in skeletal muscle?
quiz.explanation: V72: in some tissues, such as skeletal and cardiac muscle, these hormones cause vessels to dilate, increasing blood flow.

quiz.stem: In most blood vessels, epinephrine and norepinephrine cause:
quiz.explanation: V72: in most blood vessels these hormones cause constriction.

quiz.stem: Mean arterial pressure equals:
quiz.explanation: V74: MAP = CO × PR. (HR × SV is cardiac output; systolic − diastolic is pulse pressure.)

quiz.stem: Widespread vasoconstriction raises peripheral resistance while cardiac output stays the same. MAP will:
quiz.explanation: V74–V75: MAP = CO × PR, and MAP changes in response to changes in PR.

quiz.stem: MAP at birth is about:
quiz.explanation: V75: MAP is about 70 mmHg at birth.

quiz.stem: Peripheral resistance is:
options: The pressure against which the ventricles pump
The resistance to blood flow in all the blood vessels
quiz.explanation: V74: peripheral resistance is the resistance to blood flow in all the blood vessels.

quiz.stem: In the Vessels deck, baroreceptors are located in the:
quiz.explanation: V76: located in carotid sinuses and aortic arch. (Carotid and aortic BODIES are chemoreceptors, V79.)

quiz.stem: Baroreceptors respond to:
options: Stretch in arteries due to increased pressure
quiz.explanation: V76: baroreceptors respond to stretch in arteries due to increased pressure.

quiz.stem: A patient's blood pressure suddenly rises. Per Fig 13.24, which response follows?
options: ↑ parasympathetic and ↓ sympathetic stimulation; HR and SV fall and vessels dilate
↑ sympathetic stimulation; HR rises and vessels constrict
ADH is released from the hypothalamus
Renin is released from the kidneys
quiz.explanation: V78 (Fig 13.24): BP increases → baroreceptors detect → cardioregulatory center increases parasympathetic and decreases sympathetic stimulation → HR and SV decrease; vessels dilate.

quiz.stem: Chemoreceptors for the chemoreceptor reflex are located in the:
quiz.explanation: V79: chemoreceptors are located in carotid bodies and aortic bodies.

quiz.stem: Chemoreceptors are sensitive to changes in:
options: Blood oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH
quiz.explanation: V79: sensitive to changes in blood oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH.

quiz.stem: The adrenal medullary mechanism causes all of the following, EXCEPT:
options: Increased Na⁺ and water loss in urine
quiz.explanation: V81: ↑ HR, ↑ SV, vasoconstriction (and vasodilation in skeletal/cardiac muscle). Na⁺ and water loss in urine is the atrial natriuretic mechanism (V88).

quiz.stem: In the adrenal medullary mechanism, the adrenal medulla secretes:
quiz.explanation: V81: adrenal medulla secretes epinephrine and norepinephrine into blood.

quiz.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the RAAS?
options: Angiotensin II → angiotensin I → renin → ACE
Renin acts on angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → ACE → angiotensin II → aldosterone
ACE acts on renin → angiotensinogen → angiotensin II → angiotensin I
quiz.explanation: V83: renin acts on angiotensinogen to produce angiotensin I; ACE converts it to angiotensin II; angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and aldosterone release.

quiz.stem: A severely dehydrated patient has reduced blood flow to the kidneys. Which mechanism raises BP through vasoconstriction plus Na⁺ and water conservation?
quiz.explanation: V83–V84: reduced blood flow → renin; angiotensin II → vasoconstriction; aldosterone → kidneys conserve sodium and water.

quiz.stem: Angiotensin II acts on the:
quiz.explanation: V83: angiotensin II acts on adrenal cortex to release aldosterone.

quiz.stem: Aldosterone causes the kidneys to:
quiz.explanation: V84: aldosterone acts on kidneys causing them to conserve sodium and water.

quiz.stem: According to Fig 13.27, angiotensin-converting enzyme is found in the:
quiz.explanation: V85 (Fig 13.27): ACE in lung capillaries converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.

quiz.stem: A patient who hasn't had water for a day has increased plasma solute concentration. Which hormone is released and what does it do?
options: ANH; the kidneys lose Na⁺ and water
ADH; the kidneys absorb more water and urine volume decreases
quiz.explanation: V86: hypothalamic nerve cells release ADH when solute concentration increases; ADH acts on the kidneys to absorb more water (decrease urine volume).

quiz.stem: Atrial natriuretic hormone is released by:
options: The kidneys when blood flow decreases
The adrenal cortex when angiotensin II rises
Specialized cells in the right atrium when atrial blood pressure increases
quiz.explanation: V88: specialized cells in the right atrium release ANH in response to increased blood pressure in the atrium.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes ADH from ANH?
options: ADH lowers blood volume; ANH raises it
ADH decreases urine volume to maintain BP; ANH increases Na⁺ and water loss to lower BP
ADH comes from the right atrium; ANH from the hypothalamus
quiz.explanation: V86: ADH → kidneys absorb more water (↓ urine) → maintain BP. V88: ANH → loss of Na⁺ and water (↑ urine) → ↓ blood volume and BP.

quiz.stem: The effect of atrial natriuretic hormone is to:
options: Increase urine volume and decrease blood volume and blood pressure
quiz.explanation: V88: ANH promotes loss of Na⁺ and water in urine, increasing urine volume; blood volume and BP decrease.

quiz.stem: Which mechanism is most important for short-term blood pressure regulation?
quiz.explanation: V89: baroreceptor reflexes are most important for short-term regulation.

quiz.stem: All of the following are long-term blood pressure mechanisms, EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: V89: long-term control is through RAAS, ADH, and ANH; baroreceptor reflexes are short-term.

quiz.stem: Long-term blood pressure mechanisms:
options: React within seconds to large changes only
Work only through the vagus nerve
Respond gradually and are influenced by small changes in BP
quiz.explanation: V89: influenced by small changes in blood pressure and respond gradually.

quiz.stem: Atherosclerosis is:
options: A blood clot floating in the circulation
A type of arteriosclerosis from deposits of plaque in artery walls
quiz.explanation: V91: atherosclerosis — type of arteriosclerosis, from deposit of materials in artery walls (plaque).

quiz.stem: All of the following contribute to atherosclerosis, EXCEPT:
options: A diet high in cholesterol and trans fats
quiz.explanation: V91 lists lack of exercise, smoking, obesity, high cholesterol/trans-fat diet, some genetics.

quiz.stem: The anterior tibial artery becomes the:
quiz.explanation: V41: anterior tibial arteries — becomes the dorsalis pedis artery of the foot.

quiz.stem: The external iliac arteries supply the:
quiz.explanation: V39: external iliac arteries — supplies the legs.

quiz.stem: On the right side, the posterior intercostal veins drain into the:
quiz.explanation: V52: drains into azygos vein on right side; hemiazygos or accessory hemiazygos on the left.

quiz.stem: The great saphenous veins drain the:
quiz.explanation: V58: great saphenous veins drain from dorsal and medial foot.

Carries action potentials from the AV node to the ventricles
Travel down the interventricular septum to the apex
Rapidly deliver action potentials to all ventricular muscle
Includes T cells and B cells

flags.text: Slide says "Prothrombinase (clotting factor), or prothrombin is formed." Fig 11.11 (B37) shows prothrombinase and prothrombin as two separate items. The site follows the figure's three steps and does not quiz this sentence.
Slide says "95 to 85% of the population is Rh+" (the range is written backwards). Not quizzed.
Hemoglobin bullet reads only "indicates anemia". It does not say whether a low or high value indicates anemia. Not quizzed.
Normal WBC count is "5000–9000 per µL" on B54 but "5–10 thousand" per cubic mm in Fig 11.1 (B5). The site uses B54 (the test slide).

"Changes in membrane permeability are responsible for producing action potentials and called pacemaker potential." The wording is ambiguous; the slides do not define a pacemaker potential separately. Not quizzed.
Vasomotor center is "in pons and medulla oblongata" on V70, but Fig 13.23 (V77) labels "cardioregulatory and vasomotor centers in the medulla oblongata". Not quizzed on location.
Veins described as "thick with less elastic tissue and smooth muscle". Copied as written; the site only uses "less elastic tissue and smooth muscle".

Heart anatomy as text: the deck jumps to "Blood Flow through Heart 2" (no part 1). Chamber walls, heart-wall layers (endocardium/myocardium), chordae tendineae, papillary muscles, and valve structure are only figure labels or absent.
Fig 12.19 labels a "third heart sound", the "dicrotic notch", and periods of isovolumetric relaxation, but no slide explains them.
Fig 12.17 marks the PQ and QT intervals, but no slide says what they mean.
Fig 11.1 labels the buffy coat, but no slide says what it contains.
Fig 11.10 labels von Willebrand factor and ADP, but no slide explains their roles beyond the labels.
The slides say K⁺, Ca²⁺, and Na⁺ "affect cardiac function" but not how (no direction of effect).
Korotkoff sounds appear only in Fig 13.17 labels; the mechanism is not explained.
"thin later of pericardial fluid" read as "layer".
